title: OpenAI safety employee resigns, claiming the company’s ‘culture is broken’
snippet: By his own admission, David Robinson is “something of a cliché”: an employee at a leading AI company who issues a dire warning while resigning from their job.
fullText:
By his own admission, David Robinson is “something of a cliché”: an employee at a leading AI company who issues a dire warning while resigning from their job.

In an essay published in The Atlantic, Robinson said he led the writing of safety reports that accompanied OpenAI’s major product launches. He also said that with three-and-a-half years at OpenAI, he is “among the longest-tenured employees at the company.” Now he’s quitting, because in his view, the company’s “culture is broken.”

In some ways, Robinson’s comments echo those of Jacob Coxon, who worked as a researcher at both OpenAI and Anthropic before quitting and declaring that these companies are “gambling with our lives.” Coxon’s comments led to a broader debate about AI safety, with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei unveiling a plan for more cautious AI development; AI executives met with President Donald Trump this week and signed what appeared to be a hastily written, non-binding pledge to implement more safety controls.

But in Robinson’s view, the debate needs to go beyond “specific rules or new laws,” addressing the overall culture at these companies. And while much of the reporting around OpenAI has focused on how the company’s CEO Sam Altman lost the trust of former colleagues, Robinson’s essay suggests that OpenAI’s culture issues are the same as those of Silicon Valley at large.

“OpenAI has thrived by trial and error (which it calls ‘iterative deployment’), looking for problems and improving its guardrails in response,” he wrote. “But this approach, by its very nature, guarantees periodic failures — and the scale of those failures is growing as systems get more capable.”

Pointing to the recent breach of Hugging Face systems by OpenAI agents, as well as continuing revelations of OpenAI discovering more rogue agents, Robinson argued, “An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to.”

Given the increased risk, Robinson argued that frontier AI companies need to start operating “like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster.” 

But Robinson said that in his time at OpenAI, he “never encountered a colleague who had experience making airplanes fly safely or nuclear reactors run without melting down, or helping the financial system grow without collapsing.”

In response to Robinson’s essay, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company continues to improve its safety measures.

“We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” Pusateri said in a statement. “We’re making significant changes to strengthen security in our research and testing environments, train models to not just complete tasks but do so responsibly, expand our work with third-party evaluators, and improve real-time monitoring so we can detect and respond to concerning behavior earlier in the training process.”

Beyond calling for changes in OpenAI’s culture, Robinson also said it’s time to ask bigger questions about alignment — something that he admitted could sound “touchy-feely,” but he said it’s critical as companies’ current “measures of how well” AI systems “match human values are coarse.”

“The smarter the industry lets models grow while these problems remain unsolved, the more dangerous our situation becomes,” he said.

Robinson’s departure was first reported by Business Insider. In his essay, he also acknowledged that he’s following an apparently common step in the AI whistleblower playbook: He’s hired a PR firm. But he insisted, “The decision to speak out is mine alone.” 

“Perhaps I should have stayed and fought for fundamental shifts in our staffing and culture, but in practice, my colleagues and I were so busy sprinting that we seldom had the chance to consider big changes, much less to actually make them,” Robinson said. “That’s why I concluded that stronger incentives for safety — coming from outside the company — are a big part of getting this right.”

Anthony Ha is TechCrunch’s weekend editor. Previously, he worked as a tech reporter at Adweek, a senior editor at VentureBeat, a local government reporter at the Hollister Free Lance, and vice president of content at a VC firm. He lives in New York City.

title: Pixel Watch 4 & 5’s handy USB-C travel charger is currently on sale
snippet: Launched earlier this year, that useful little USB-C charger dongle for Google’s Pixel Watch 4 and Pixel Watch 5 smartwatches is currently discounted. more…
fullText:
Launched earlier this year, that useful little USB-C charger dongle for Google’s Pixel Watch 4 and Pixel Watch 5 smartwatches is currently discounted.

Google’s latest take on smartwatch charging debuted on last year’s Pixel Watch 4 series, with two pins popping out of the smartwatch to connect with a magnetic dock. Google’s official charging cable works well enough, but it’s just another thing to plug in when you’re traveling. 

Wasserstein, a long-time Made for Google accessory partner, launched a handy alternative earlier this year. A simple charger that attaches to the end of any USB-C cable give you the option to cut down on some bulk while still being able to easily top off your smartwatch on the go. Its price was in flux for quite a while, but eventually settled at $30.

Right now, though, it’s discounted to $25. Not a huge discount, but it certainly makes the handy charger an easier buy if you have any travel coming up through the end of the year.

	

Wasserstein USB-C charger for Pixel Watch 4 & 5 at Amazon

As a reminder, this works with all Pixel Watch 4 and Pixel Watch 5 smartwatches, regardless of if you’re using the 41mm or 45mm sizes. You’ll want to plug into at least 7.5W of power, but you’re likely getting that from whatever charger you’re using with your smartphone anyway. Just keep in mind that Pixel Watch 3 and prior cannot use this charger.

title: Fitbit Air launches in India later this week
snippet: Google is expanding the Fitbit Air to India later this week following a global launch earlier this year. more…
fullText:
Google is expanding the Fitbit Air to India later this week following a global launch earlier this year.

Available starting on October 2, the Fitbit Air will arrive in India for ₹13,999. That’s around $145 USD when directly converted, but that’s roughly in line with the conversion on Pixel Watch 5 pricing in the region too. 

Google says:

Fitbit Air will be on shelves at the Google Store and our retail partners on 2 October for ₹13,999. It comes in four colorways — Obsidian, Berry, Lavender and Fog — and includes a three-month trial of Google Health Premium, giving you full access to Google Health Coach right out of the box. 

Fitbit Air will be available in India through the Google Store and presumably at retailers such as Flipkart. As it stands, it doesn’t look like the Stephen Curry edition will be sold in India, but the core colors and band options are all on their way.

title: YouTube says Shorts recommendations won’t surface unoriginal content
snippet: YouTube says it wants to ‘focus on originality’ in a push to surface better Shorts recommendations for users. more…
fullText:
YouTube says it wants to ‘focus on originality’ in a push to surface better Shorts recommendations for users.

Shorts is built on quick and attention-grabbing content, which makes cutting portions of long-form videos one of the easiest ways to put out quick videos with high view potential. Of course, that also means channels can just as easily take content from other established creators and stamp out short-form videos from it.

YouTube says it’s adjusted its Shorts recommendations so users will see less unoriginal content. Users who upload content that blatantly steals video from another channel will not get the same reach as they did before the change, according to what YouTube laid out in its release.

To improve the Shorts experience for everyone, we’re updating our recommendation systems to further prioritize original content and reduce the reach of content re-uploaded from other creators without adding anything of your own.

There’s a small amount of room for interpretation. YouTube’s language seems to imply that Shorts that contain no changes form another’s work would be affected, but no clear line in the sand has been drawn out.

	

Remember, YouTube announced it was testing a new feature that would let users reimagine other channels’ videos using AI, which was released in March. Whether those videos will still be surfaced in the recommendations system is unclear.

The change should mean users will see a focus on original content, and creators that upload original Shorts will likely be rewarded. YouTube hasn’t detailed a rollout date for this change, but it sounds like it may be live already.

title: iOS 27 breaks 15 years of muscle memory on iPhone and iPad
snippet: Since iOS 5 in 2011, the iPhone and iPad have included Notification Center, a central place to find alerts from various apps in chronological order. Starting with iOS 27, Apple is making a major change to how users open Notification Center on iPhone and iPad. iOS 27 is here after a summer of beta releases. The behavior changed slightly between the first two releases. However, this change shipped, and I’m still adjusting to it. more…
fullText:
Since iOS 5 in 2011, the iPhone and iPad have included Notification Center, a central place to find alerts from various apps in chronological order.

Starting with iOS 27, Apple is making a major change to how users open Notification Center on iPhone and iPad.

iOS 27 is here after a summer of beta releases. The behavior changed slightly between the first two releases. However, this change shipped, and I’m still adjusting to it.

Siri AI takes over the swipe gesture for a lot of the iPhone and iPad top edge

Opening Notification Center is unchanged on iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 by default. However, enabling Siri AI changes a key swipe gesture on both iPhone and iPad.

One of the many ways of invoking Siri AI, once enabled, is by swiping down from the center of the top edge of your iPhone or iPad display. This previously opened Notification Center.

You can still access Notification Center by swiping down from the top-left corner once Siri AI is enabled. Alerts now animate in from the top left corner. This is a way to point users toward Notification Center’s smaller surface area.

Apple is greatly prioritizing Siri AI access in iOS 27. The majority of the top edge is devoted to invoking the new Siri experience.

The last time Apple made a change to accessing Notification Center came when Control Center moved from a swipe up gesture from the bottom to a top-right corner swipe down gesture on iPhone X. Apple later unified this experience across devices.

Notifications now live in the top left corner

Now it’s Notification Center’s turn to be put in the corner. On iPadOS 27 beta 1 in particular, the area above Home screen app icons was pretty much devoted to invoking Siri AI. The area for opening Notification Center actually shrank if you disable displaying AM/PM or the date.

	

Apple improved this with iPadOS 27 beta 2, creating a more uniform region on either side. It’s roughly the size of two app columns with Notification Center on the left and Control Center on the right. The rest is for invoking Siri. 

After 15 years of muscle memory, it’ll take some time to determine if this change is worth it or something that should be reconsidered. In the meantime, early feedback sounds overwhelmingly positive around Apple’s new Siri AI system. Hearing that Siri is good now will also take some getting used to, I’m sure.

After months of using the new behavior, I’m certain I’d toggle it off if there were a setting to do so. Since there’s no option to disable invoking Siri from the top middle swipe down, the only thing to do is build new muscle memory around avoiding the center.

What do you think? Would you change this back if you could? Is accessing Siri from the swipe-down gesture worth the change? Share your thoughts in the comments.

title: This fake Mac Zoom installer has a sneaky way to bypass Gatekeeper
snippet: Cybersecurity company Jamf has discovered a fake Mac installer for the videoconferencing app Zoom that uses a sneaky way to bypass Apple’s Gatekeeper protection against malware. The malware does actually install Zoom, but also an infostealer that captures data and sends it to the attacker’s server … more…
fullText:
Cybersecurity company Jamf has discovered a fake Mac installer for the videoconferencing app Zoom that uses a sneaky way to bypass Apple’s Gatekeeper protection against malware.

The malware does actually install Zoom, but also an infostealer that captures data and sends it to the attacker’s server …

Normally, when you try to install a Mac app that Apple hasn’t notarized, macOS will refuse to open it. There is a workaround to allow you to do so, but it’s somewhat fiddly, and attackers have to find some way to persuade users to do it.

The criminals behind the malware Jamf has dubbed CloudSyncD have found a clever way to make this seem more normal to users. The app installer dropper includes a background image with instructions, as shown above.

CloudSyncD arrives as a disk image that mounts as a volume named Zoom, laid out to look like any ordinary Mac installer: an application icon on the left, an alias to Applications on the right. The difference is the background image, which carries a numbered Setup list telling the victim to open System Settings, go to Privacy & Security, scroll to the Security section, click Open Anyway, and enter their administrator password. Those are instructions to bypass Gatekeeper.

You kind of have to admire the creativity of this.

Once the malware is installed, it can record user-entered data and send it to the attackers as frequently as every eight seconds.

As always, you should only ever install Mac apps from the official Mac App Store or the websites of developers you trust.

CNN CEO Mark Thompson will remain at the head of the news network when Paramount’s $110 billion Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition closes this week. Thompson wrote in a memo to employees that he believes the combined company will “fully support the principle and practice of the kind of independent news that CNN has always stood for,” according to a report from The New York Times. The news comes as part of an announcement detailing the combined company’s executive leadership.

Paramount CEO David Ellison will lead the companies — to be called Skydance — alongside former Mattel head Ynon Kreiz. Speculation about what would become of CNN swirled following the news of the media megamerger, which puts WBD’s CNN and Paramount’s CBS News under the same roof. As part of a settlement reached with 12 states, Skydance must adopt a news editorial independence board.

The entertainment giant revealed the rest of its executive lineup as well, with HBO CEO Casey Bloys serving as the chief content officer of Skydance’s streaming business. Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg will head up Skydance’s film studios, while George Cheeks will run its TV business. Bari Weiss, who was appointed editor-in-chief of CBS News last year, will remain in her role even as ratings decline.

Paramount’s acquisition is expected to close on Tuesday.

title: Apple’s new ‘homeOS’ will launch this month, here’s what’s coming
snippet: Apple reportedly plans to launch new Home products on October 13 alongside an all-new operating system rumored to be called ‘homeOS.’ Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple reportedly plans to launch new Home products on October 13 alongside an all-new operating system rumored to be called ‘homeOS.’ Here are the details.

homeOS will run on new ‘HomePad’ product, featuring mix of other Apple OS designs

Apple’s highly anticipated ‘HomePad’ smart home hub is reportedly being unveiled on October 13. And per Mark Gurman, it will run on a brand new operating system that’s rumored to be called ‘homeOS.’

A recent Bloomberg report offers a lot of details on what to expect from homeOS. It reportedly features a blend of other Apple OS designs, including:

iPhone-style widgets

iPad-like app designs

Apple Watch-style icons for its Home Screen 

The default UI, per Gurman, “is built heavily around photo slideshows and clock displays, similar to the new StandBy Mode on the upcoming iPhone Duo” and users can “swipe up from the clock screen or photos to open the app launcher.”

We’ve seen multiple leaks this past week around this Photo Face in homeOS, as seen below.

Siri AI is the central input method, but Apple apps and a Home Screen will also be available via touch

Siri AI will be central to homeOS interactions. Per Gurman on his new podcast:

The new operating system is basically, what would an OS look like if Siri AI had an OS? If Siri AI was not just an app on the phone, if it wasn’t just an interface on the phone. What if it was an operating system?…It’s all about this concept of personal search and personal context, being able to ask for songs, podcasts, notes, calendar items, photos that are bespoke to you.

Voice won’t be the only interaction method though. Apple apps and a Home Screen will be part of homeOS too. Siri AI can be used to control these apps, but touch input will be supported too.

Built-in homeOS apps will include Music, Podcasts, Photos, Weather, FaceTime, Notes, Calendar, Messages, Reminders, and more. No App Store is expected to be available, but third-party widgets can be brought over from your iPhone.

Like on the current HomePod though, the idea is that most of the time, your interactions with homeOS happen via Siri.

title: iPadOS 27.2: Two new features coming soon to your iPad
snippet: iPadOS 27.2 is coming later this month as a new iPad software update, here are two new features it will bring. more…
fullText:
iPadOS 27.2 is coming later this month as a new iPad software update, here are two new features it will bring.

Siri AI is a major improvement over the old Siri, and I’m using it all the time on my iPad—often with a CMD + Space keyboard shortcut since Siri and Spotlight are now integrated.

In iPadOS 27.2, Apple is introducing another convenient way to interact with Siri that first debuted on the Mac in macOS Golden Gate.

When you select text in iPadOS 27.2 via a trackpad or mouse, there’s a new Siri contextual popup that appears to the left of your selection. If you hover over the Siri icon with your cursor, it instantly expands to offer an ‘Ask Siri’ text field.

This makes it quick and easy to ask Siri about whatever you’ve highlighted. And if you’re in the writing process, the Siri popup even has suggestions like ‘Proofread,’ ‘Rewrite,’ and ‘How does this sound?’ so you can get help with just a click.

#2: Profiles in Apple TV app

iPads make great video devices whether you’re an adult or a kid. And if you share an iPad with a partner or child, the Apple TV app has a welcome addition coming soon: user profiles.

iPadOS 27.2 brings over the same profiles feature that tvOS already offers on Apple TV 4K.

When you open the Apple TV app on iPad, you’ll see a new profile selection screen at startup. From here, you can choose who’s watching and the TV app will automatically update its queue, playback history, and content recommendations based on your selection.

If you’re a parent, profiles will take content restrictions into account. So when your child’s profile is active, they’ll only see films and TV shows that match the age settings you’ve previously set.

title: Vessev built an electric ferry that almost flies
snippet: Vessev hopes its electric hydrofoil ferry will change the way people and cities think about boats.
fullText:
“When will we start flying?” I asked Vessev co-founder and CEO Eric Laakmann, as we pulled away from the Brooklyn marina in the startup’s VS-9 electric ferry. “We already are.”

I’ll admit I was a bit disappointed. I thought the moment when it transitioned from sailing like a regular boat to almost-flying as a surface-skimming hydrofoil would be more … momentous. 

I’ve been on my share of boats, including large ferries, small sailboats, and plenty of others in between, but I’d never been on a hydrofoil and I was curious what flying along the water might feel like during the brief ride from the Brooklyn Marina out toward Governors Island on the East River in New York.

It didn’t feel like flying, but it was a bit like riding in a sports car.

The wake when foiling in the VS-9 is minimalImage Credits:Tim De Chant/TechCrunch

Traditional boats of this size — about 30 feet — start to bounce and slap the water as they gain speed. But on a hydrofoil, that’s when the foils start to do their work.

On the surface, the VS-9 looks like plenty of other catamarans. But under the hull are two wing-like structures that lift the boat as they slice through the water. Computer-controlled underwater flaps keep the ride smooth and stable. In the VS-9, most of the lifting is done by the front foil, with about 20% handled by the rear.

The VS-9 can raise its foils to access docks in shallower watersImage Credits:Tim De Chant/TechCrunch

The rear foil also hosts the electric motor, which Vessev makes in-house. Why not outsource it? Laakmann said that it’s important to keep costs in line — eventually, you’ll have to bring production in-house, so why not do it earlier in development? The only thing Vessev doesn’t build are the batteries. “Those have been commoditized,” Laakmann said.

By lifting the hull clear of the water, hydrofoils can operate more efficiently than other boats. That’s especially important for electric boats, where every kilowatt-hour counts.

Shipbuilders have been experimenting with hydrofoils for well over a century. The design offers several advantages, including lower drag and a smoother ride. The subtle transition I experienced on the VS-9, from sailing to almost-flying, underlined just how smooth a hydrofoil can be.

The Vessev VS-9 can charge using a typical EV chargerImage Credits:Tim De Chant/TechCrunch

Despite hydrofoils’ advantages, they’re not a panacea. The design works best in waters the boat can clear when sailing on its foils. For the VS-9, that’s about two and a half feet, or 0.75 meters. If the waves go higher than that, they start hitting the hull, ruining the smooth ride and sapping some efficiency. While they’re not ideal for the open ocean, hydrofoils make sense for other waterways, including lakes, rivers, and bays. 

Vessev, which raised a $19 million Series A in August, is targeting transit operations to start. Laakmann thinks the combination of electric propulsion and hydrofoils can bring down the cost of operating smaller vessels and make them comfortable enough that they could augment urban mass transit systems. 

Somewhere like New York City could use them to zip people to Brooklyn or Queens without needing to build much new infrastructure.

The VS-9 can carry a full passenger load up to 40 nautical miles (46 miles or 74 kilometers)Image Credits:Tim De Chant/TechCrunch

Hotels and tour operators are also an early target market, and public demonstrations like the one I attended have attracted wealthy individuals looking for another toy, Laakmann said.

For now, the VS-9 I rode is one of a kind, but Laakmann said Vessev plans to build more. Eventually, the company might shift to producing electric hydrofoil kits, allowing other boatbuilders to design their own vessels around the technology, Laakmann said.

title: Googlebooks with Intel chipsets might have trouble with ‘complex’ Android apps
snippet: According to a statement from Google, Intel-based Googlebooks will apparently still struggle with some Android apps. more…
fullText:
According to a statement from Google, Intel-based Googlebooks will apparently still struggle with some Android apps.

When Android apps made their debut on ChromeOS, one of the big downsides was that ARM-based machines ran those apps better than those using Intel chips. It was never a surprise given that Android apps are generally designed for devices running on an ARM architecture vs the x86 used on Intel chips.

Yet, the problem remains on Googlebook.

Despite the whole platform being Android-based this time around, Google confirmed in a statement to Android Authority that Intel-based Googlebook machines will still run into the occasional hiccup with “complex” Android apps and games, though the company emphasizes that “the vast majority” will work just fine.

	

The vast majority of Android apps run smoothly across both Intel and Qualcomm Googlebooks right out of the box.

Because many Android apps were originally designed for Arm chips, a small handful of complex apps or games need some developer tuning to run their best on Intel-based platforms. We’re working hand-in-hand with app developers, Intel, and Qualcomm to continuously optimize performance and expand compatibility across the entire portfolio.

Still, this is noteworthy as the first wave of Googlebook hardware includes mostly Intel-based machines. Laptops from Lenovo, Asus, and Acer all run on Panther Lake-generation Intel chips, while Dell and HP machines both use the Snapdragon X Elite (the 2024 chip, not the newer version).

Another chip used for Googlebook from MediaTek is also in the works, though no machines are using it just yet.

The first batch of Googlebook laptops are all available as of today.

title: Apple Watch Series 12, Ultra 4 adding two new features soon
snippet: Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 have arrived, and later this year they’ll get even more powerful with two new features: Siri Recap and Live Rewind. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 have arrived, and later this year they’ll get even more powerful with two new features: Siri Recap and Live Rewind. Here are the details.

#1: Siri Recap

Siri AI is a major tentpole of watchOS 27, and later this year there’s a powerful Siri addition coming to Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. It’s called Siri Recap.

Here’s what it does, per Apple:

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment. Your summaries auto-delete after 7 days if you choose not to save them.

Siri Recap seems like the kind of feature that no one was necessarily asking for, but it could add valuable utility if the privacy protections are done right. You can read the finer details around privacy in Apple’s white paper here.

#2: Live Rewind

Live Rewind is another ‘Audio Intelligence’ feature coming to the new Apple Watch models later this year. It provides a more direct way to revisit something that was just said.

Here’s how it works per Apple:

Live Rewind recalls what was just said in the last 15 seconds by showing a text snippet on your Apple Watch when you double-press the Digital Crown, so you can catch something you missed or are less familiar with. You can ask Siri about the content of the snippet or simply save it to the Siri app.

Like Siri Recap, Apple has in-depth details on Live Rewind’s privacy protections outlined here. For me personally, the utility of Live Rewind seems less obvious beyond accessibility needs. But I’m interested to see how it works in its finished form.

What do you think of the Siri Recap and Live Rewind features coming to Apple Watch? Let us know in the comments.

title: Galaxy S27 series pricing may not only increase, but cost more to upgrade storage
snippet: Samsung’s new Galaxy S27 series is rumored to come at a higher price than previous versions, but that’s no surprise. What’s a little harder to swallow is the larger rumored gap between storage variants, according to one leaker. more…
fullText:
Samsung’s new Galaxy S27 series is rumored to come at a higher price than previous versions, but that’s no surprise. What’s a little harder to swallow is the larger rumored gap between storage variants, according to one leaker.

In succession to the Galaxy S26 lineup, the Galaxy S27 series is expected to take on plenty of physical changes. Namely, in design. Previous leaks have provided CAD renders of the new camera island and overall look, but those have also been caveated with a promised price increase.

Following rumors that the Galaxy S27 Ultra could start at $1,400, a new bit of information has surfaced from a leaker on Naver. According to Lanzuk, the Galaxy S27 series, as a whole, is expected to come at a higher price. The estimated jump is reportedly in the “high 130,000 won range” (~$100). But the post also suggests Samsung is setting a “steeper rate of increase” to the prices of each capacity, likely referring to storage variants.

That could suggest that, instead of a $200 gap between some storage variants, the disparity could expand. Then again, the post isn’t clear on whether this is a linear price increase or one that also increases upgrade costs over previous generations.

	

The posted leak is courtesy of domestic Korean sources, indicating this price increase is specific to Samsung’s home soil. That doesn’t mean it won’t translate to other regions, like the US or Europe.

We’re a bit wary of a report like this. Not because a price increase is unlikely for the Galaxy S27 series – statistically, it very much is – but because of clashing numbers. The previously noted leak also suggested the Galaxy S27 series would remain unchanged as a whole, apart from the most premium flagship model. This leak contradicts that, noting every device will see a jump.

It’s very possible that Samsung is flipping between the two until it ultimately decides on exactly how much it needs to increase the cost of each device and variant to make a profit off of devices stuffed with NAND and LPDDR6 RAM, which the post also notes will be included on “some models.”

Until the Galaxy S27 series launches early next year, there will likely be little confirmation on Samsung’s finalized price increases.

title: California Legalized Plug-In Balcony Solar Panels, but Don’t Buy Any Just Yet
snippet: Units that comply with the new law are expected by spring.
fullText:
Energy prices are high, no matter what state you live in, but they’re especially high in sunny California. Homeowners in the Golden State have been able to get some relief by installing solar panels to defray their electric bill, and now renters and apartment dwellers can, too, as California officially legalized plug-in balcony solar panels this week. But don’t go buy a kit just yet. 

The so-called Plug and Play Solar Act (Senate Bill No. 868), signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom and sponsored by state Sen. Scott Wiener, permits the use of plug-in solar for apartments, condos and single-family homes, as long as it meets the regulations in the bill.

“This new law will deliver cleaner power, greater energy independence and real savings for consumers,” Bernadette Del Chiaro, senior vice president for California at the nonprofit Environmental Working Group, said in a statement.

Plug-in solar units don’t have to go on balconies.

Zoltux

Until the passage of bills like this, installing solar panels required you to have an interconnection agreement for anything with the potential to put power back into the grid. In the case of California, the process of completing an interconnection agreement required an upfront cost of $100 to $800 and would take an hour, with approval typically taking three days, according to PG&E.

			

More from CNET

While the process has been simplified, the new law still has some requirements. The solar system can’t generate more than 1,200 watts per home, which is about enough to power a window AC unit. You also need to register the balcony solar kit, like it’s a rooftop panel system, and it needs to be certified by an outside safety organization. It also needs to be configured not to feed power back into the grid during a power outage, potentially through the use of a separate smart power management meter, such as the Smart Gateway Lite from Mango Power.

Jackery’s SolarVault system works for balcony solar.Ajay Kumar/CNET

Plug-in solar panels can be installed almost anywhere there’s open space and a standard AC outlet. The big advantage of them is that you can deploy them in a backyard, on a balcony or on a roof without having to do the expensive wiring and installation of rooftop solar panels. This technology has been popular in Europe, especially in Germany, where 4 million systems have been installed, but it’s also making steady inroads in the US.

Dozens of US states are considering or have already passed legislation to legalize balcony solar. According to the Environmental Working Group, California is the 10th state to legalize balcony solar, effectively doubling the size of the US market. The first to pass the law was Utah, which did so in March 2025. A more recent one was New Jersey, where Gov. Mikie Sherrill signed a bill that would prevent landlords and local governments from blocking residents and tenants from installing solar panels with a maximum power output of 1,200 watts.

Bluetti showed off its balcony solar system at IFA Berlin 2026.Ajay Kumar/CNET

The passage of this law may be a tipping point for balcony solar. When I was at IFA Berlin 2026 in September, I saw several balcony solar systems from Jackery, EcoFlow, Bluetti and others, with a Bluetti representative specifically informing me that they were waiting for some uncertainty around US regulations to be resolved before releasing in the US market.

A representative from Mango Power, which makes solar kits and home backups, told me last year that it was difficult to advise US customers on what solutions are available for their specific states because, ultimately, consumers need to be clear about the regulations before buying.

None of the units currently on the market meet California’s requirements, so you can’t just go out and buy one right now if you’re a California resident. The systems will still need to be registered as rooftop solar systems. Noncompliant systems will also become illegal in the state in 2030, though the groups sponsoring the bill expect that models that are compliant with California’s requirements will come to market in the spring. 

Various balcony solar manufacturers did not immediately respond to requests for comment regarding the availability of California-compliant units.

title: What has been the best Google Pixel to date? [Poll]
snippet: On 4 October 2016, Google introduced the original Pixel and Pixel XL, marking a major pivot away from the developer-focused Nexus line and ushering in what is now a decade of “Made by Google” hardware – but which is best and why? more…
fullText:
On 4 October 2016, Google introduced the original Pixel and Pixel XL, marking a major pivot away from the developer-focused Nexus line and ushering in what is now a decade of “Made by Google” hardware – but which is best and why?

Over the past 10 years, the lineup has expanded from a pair of traditional slab smartphones to a product portfolio that includes foldable devices, watches, earbuds, a single tablet, and budget-focused A-series models, culminating in the Pixel 11 series.

I’m biased, I think that the 4a is the best of the bunch, but determining which device holds the title of the best Pixel to date is going to be a fun, healthy debate for those of us who have used more than a few of the lineup over the years, especially as not all have been covered in glory.

The initial breakthrough

The original Pixel and Pixel XL established Google’s focus on camera processing and clean software integration. While the launch models lacked water resistance and stereophonic audio, their computational photography capabilities set a new baseline for mobile imaging.

	

A year later, the Pixel 2 and Pixel 2 XL introduced the iconic “Panda” design and front-facing stereo speakers. Although the LG-manufactured Pixel 2 XL faced criticism regarding display viewing angles, the series remains highly regarded for solidifying Google’s image processing dominance.

The Pixel 3 and 3 XL introduced Night Sight and a dedicated Pixel Visual Core chip, alongside dual front-facing cameras with an ultra-wide sensor. Despite memory management limits tied to its 4GB of RAM and the prominent display notch on the XL model, the third-generation devices brought significant refinements to software performance. Shortly after, the Pixel 3a series created the mid-range budget category for Google, pairing flagship camera capabilities with lower price points.

Pivots, Experiments, and Design Changes

Google shifted its approach with the Pixel 4 and 4 XL, introducing Soli radar gesture controls, 90Hz Motion Sense displays, and the only instance of 3D Face Unlock. The removal of the rear fingerprint scanner and poor battery life on the smaller model limited its appeal, though the 4 XL maintains a loyal following for its build, slim profile, and biometric features.

The 4a and 4a 5G focused back on value during a period of transition. That path culminated in the Pixel 5, which abandoned high-end flagship processors in favor of a mid-range Qualcomm Snapdragon 765G chipset, a uniform-bezel design, a rear fingerprint sensor, and a high-density battery. The Pixel 5a with 5G followed a similar template with a larger form factor and water resistance.

The Pixel 6 and 6 Pro marked the biggest moment in the lineup since its inception. Introducing custom Google Tensor silicon, a horizontal camera bar design, the series briefly pushed Google back into true flagship territory. The subsequent Pixel 6a brought this design language and processor to the A-series lineup, but had the killer addition of the best Tensor chip at a time when most mid-rangers were still forgoing high-end SoCs in favor of middling performance.

Refinement continued with the Pixel 7 and 7 Pro, which upgraded to the Tensor G2, addressed thermal efficiency, and refreshed the camera bar with an aluminum finish. The 7a brought high-refresh-rate screens and wireless charging to the lower price bracket for the first time.

Expanding Form Factors and Beyond

Google’s smartphone ecosystem expanded significantly with the introduction of the Pixel Fold and the Pixel Tablet. The Fold represented Google’s entry into flexible displays with a wider outer screen, while the Pixel Tablet offered a dual-purpose home display experience via its charging speaker dock.

The Pixel 8 and 8 Pro introduced seven years of OS updates, Tensor G3 silicon, brighter Actua displays, and a flat screen design for the Pro model. The 8a brought those long-term software commitments to a lower price point and arguably blurred the lines between the A-series and the base model for the first time.

	

The Pixel 9 series expanded the lineup further, introducing a third flagship size with the Pixel 9, Pixel 9 Pro, and Pixel 9 Pro XL, alongside the refined Pixel 9 Pro Fold. The series introduced updated industrial design with flattened sides, updated Tensor G4 chips, and satellite connectivity.

Since the 9 was launched, we’ve had a couple of years of effectively the same device with minor iterations. Most of the changes have been focused solely on hardware efficiency and processing performance.

Reaching the 10-year mark, the Pixel 11 series builds upon that decade of iterations. From off-the-shelf components to custom chips that may not have quite hit the heights many have wanted, there’s never a dull moment with a Google phone, for better or worse.

Which device stands out as the best release over the last 10 years? We’ve omitted wearables in a bid to streamline the entire poll, but be sure to cast your vote in the poll below and let us know the reasons behind your choice in the comments.

title: Ready for Driverless Trucks? I Took a Ride in Kodiak’s Autonomous Semi
snippet: Kodiak is planning to bring its fully self-driving trucks to highways later this year. I took a test ride to see the technology in action.
fullText:
Despite the growing number of players in the space, self-driving vehicles remain far from ubiquitous. In places like the San Francisco Bay Area, hailing a robotaxi is now nearly as easy as requesting an Uber. But in most cities, driverless cars have yet to surface at all.

Still, autonomous vehicles of all sizes and purposes continue to crop up in various regions. Kodiak AI is one company looking to shake up transportation and shipping in the near future. Founded in 2018, it set out to deploy semi trucks on highways without a human behind the wheel, and it’s getting close to realizing that vision.

The company’s autonomous driving system, called the Kodiak Driver, launched in December 2024, and has so far been deployed in 35 fully driverless trucks, which are owned and operated by Atlas Energy Solutions in the Permian Basin in New Mexico and Texas. The trucks haul frac sand, typically used during hydraulic fracking to help keep fractures in rock formations open, from depots to well sites.

Kodiak plans to deploy its self-driving trucks on highways in Texas by the end of the year.Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Now, Kodiak wants to bring its fully driverless operations to the highway, starting in Texas with services for furniture giant Ikea later this year. That route will operate between Houston and Dallas, spanning 219 miles primarily along Interstate 45.

Massive trucks barreling down highways without a driver may be a daunting vision, but Michael Wiesinger, Kodiak’s chief operating officer, says they’ll make transportation more reliable and efficient.

“Lots of people, unfortunately, are getting killed in traffic, and many of those are related to truck accidents,” he said. “An autonomous truck [has a] 360-degree view of the world, [and] will actually never get drowsy, never get tired, never get distracted. They will make transportation safer.”

This is the sensor pod that houses the cameras, lidar and radar.Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

In California, Kodiak’s driverless tech is already being used to ship produce from Fresno to Los Angeles, though a safety driver remains behind the wheel, ready to take over as needed.

I visited Kodiak’s headquarters in Mountain View, California, to ride in one of the company’s trucks and see its autonomous tech in action. As per current state regulations, there was still a safety operator onboard, ready to take control of the wheel if necessary. I wasn’t exactly nervous, but his presence nevertheless helped to assuage any trepidation, given how much bigger a semi truck is than a robotaxi from Waymo or Zoox.

During the demonstration, the Kodiak truck easily navigated surface streets, including making tight turns and dodging rows of parallel-parked cars and trailers. We made our way to the highway on-ramp rather slowly and carefully, picking up speed to 55 mph once we hit the roadway. When we really got going, it all felt remarkably ordinary, with the truck weaving through lanes and dodging construction cones without any trouble. After about 20 minutes, the truck navigated to an exit and we made our way back to Kodiak’s HQ. 

Kodiak’s trucks run on diesel — the standard for heavy-duty commercial trucking — which allows them to travel over longer distances than if they were electric, the company notes.

The inside of the Kodiak semi feels standard — apart from the screen showing what the vehicle sees as it navigates autonomously.Celso Bulgatti/CNET

The growth of driverless operations brings with it mounting concern about lost jobs. Kodiak says deploying autonomous vehicles doesn’t mean humans won’t be involved at all.

“Before launching an autonomous truck, it gets inspected, it gets fueled, it gets prepared for the run,” Wiesinger said. “Those preparations are done by humans on the ground.”

He added that Kodiak is collaborating with truck-stop providers to help with refueling as it plans to eventually expand its driverless range across thousands of miles.

Kodiak isn’t the only company working on autonomous trucking. Other players include Aurora, Waabi and Gatik, while Tesla is making a push into this space as well with its all-electric Tesla Semi, which could one day adopt driverless capabilities, too.

Before climbing aboard Kodiak’s semi, it was hard to fathom how a Class 8 heavy-duty truck could navigate the complexities of residential streets and highways. As we passed other cars, I found myself wondering whether those drivers and passengers realized they were sharing the road with what could be the future of long-haul trucking. Then again, some of those folks were cruising in a Waymo robotaxi, so perhaps the existence of autonomous trucks won’t be such a tough pill to swallow for everyone.

Check out the video above for my ride-along in Kodiak’s self-driving truck.

title: Trump unveils his new Super Intelligence Force
snippet: This new task force is Trump's latest response to the debate over AI safety.
fullText:
As promised, President Donald Trump has announced the formation of a new Super Intelligence Force, which he said will be led by national intelligence director Jay Clayton and other members of his administration.

“The Super Intelligence Force is tasked with coordinating the effort of the Federal Government to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans,” Trump said in a Sunday morning post on his social network Truth Social.

Back in September, in response to an AI safety debate that the president has largely dismissed as a hoax created by “Radical Left Dumocrats,” Trump said he would nevertheless form an AI Force and appoint an AI czar (“Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!”).

Since then, Trump signed an executive order seeking to rebrand AI as “super intelligence,” a term seemingly embraced, with some stumbles, by the tech executives who gathered at the White House this week to sign a non-binding safety pledge. (The pledge included an impressive typo.) 

So it’s only natural that Trump’s new task force is named in accordance with this new branding. The Wall Street Journal reports that Clayton will chair the Super Intelligence Force, effectively making him the new AI/SI czar, with Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, Undersecretary of War for Research and Engineering Emil Michael, and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor serving as vice chairs.

The task force will reportedly have 120 days to create a report on the risks and opportunities presented by AI. Clayton, who previously said that it would be irresponsible for the United States to “back away” from AI while countries like China advance, made similar comments to the WSJ, insisting that one of the biggest risks is “not being first.”

The task force’s charter reportedly says that it will “develop plans for responding to SI-enabled threats to our society, while preventing overregulation and regulatory capture that would stifle innovation and competition.”

title: iPhone 18 Pro Max Can’t Make a Call on AT&T? Apple Says It Will Replace It for Free
snippet: A software and carrier settings update should prevent future problems, but people who have been affected will need a replacement phone.
fullText:
Some owners of Apple’s new iPhone 18 Pro Max may be enjoying the new camera system and improved battery life. But if they’re AT&T customers, they could find the phone unable to perform its most essential task: making calls. That also includes being able to dial 911 in emergencies. The fix appears to be a pair of Apple updates rolling out on Friday – but anyone who has already been affected by the problem will need a replacement phone, according to Apple. An Apple representative says the company will replace those phones for free.

Last week, some iPhone 18 Pro Max owners on AT&T’s network reported no cellular access. MacRumors reported that AT&T sent a text message this week to iPhone 18 Pro Max owners, encouraging them to update to iOS 27.0.1 immediately. MacRumors estimates that thousands of customers have been affected.

On Friday, Apple said it’s issuing a separate carrier-settings patch to pair with the iOS 27.0.1 update. But the patch comes too late for certain owners of the new phone.

			

More from CNET

An Apple representative told CNET that the updates are intended to guard against this problem in the future and won’t fix the situation for iPhone 18 Pro Max owners who are already experiencing it. Apple will provide a new phone free of charge to those owners. Affected customers should contact Apple Support or AT&T.

In Reddit threads about the issue, some owners report that the 27.0.1 update by itself did not fix the problem, nor did upgrading to the public beta of iOS 27.2.

Only the iPhone 18 Pro Max is affected

So far, the issue seems limited to iPhone 18 Pro Max models on AT&T’s network. I reached out to contacts at T-Mobile and Verizon, and both report they’re not seeing similar reports on their networks. I haven’t experienced the issue on an iPhone 18 Pro that runs on AT&T’s network, which isn’t surprising given that this particular problem affects iPhone 18 Pro Max units, not iPhone 18 Pro phones. A CNET colleague’s iPhone 18 Pro Max on Google Fi (which uses T-Mobile’s network) is not experiencing the issue.

It’s unclear whether the lack of connectivity is related to the phone’s hardware. While the standard iPhone 18 Pro is equipped with Apple’s C2 modem, the iPhone 18 Pro Max in the US is the only model with Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X80 modem, as shown in this teardown of the phone by iFixIt. Qualcomm has been Apple’s modem provider for years, but Apple has worked to move away from relying on the third party for the essential phone component. That relationship is due to expire this year.

According to a TechInsights iPhone 18 Pro Max teardown, the X80 modem is also used in the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max, but a new millimeter-wave antenna has been added to the 18 Pro Max. Millimeter-wave offers much faster data speeds in areas where the technology is installed, but it can have a shorter range and be reduced by obstacles. Apple’s C2 modem also includes a millimeter-wave antenna.

A representative from Qualcomm didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: The iPhone 18 Pro is selling well in China for three reasons
snippet: A new market intelligence report says that the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are selling well in China, making Apple the best-selling brand in the country during the launch week. Counterpoint Research has said there are three reasons for the popularity of Apple’s latest iPhone … more…
fullText:
A new market intelligence report says that the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are selling well in China, making Apple the best-selling brand in the country during the launch week.

Counterpoint Research has said there are three reasons for the popularity of Apple’s latest iPhone … 

Rising costs have seen overall sales of new smartphones in China decline 17% year on year since July, according to Counterpoint Research’s China Weekly Smartphone Sell-Out Tracker. However, the firm reports that this trend was reversed by the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro.

During the first three days of its sales (which accounted for only three days in Week 38), the iPhone 18 Pro series recorded 12% YoY growth compared with the iPhone sales. The strong initial performance helped Apple move into the No. 1 spot in sales in Week 38, with a 33% share of China’s smartphone market.

Three reasons for success

Counterpoint suggests there are three reasons underlying the popularity of the new model.

First, the delayed launch of the base iPhone 18. Because Apple has launched the two iPhone 18 Pro models well ahead of the standard model, some may have decided to upgrade to the premium version rather than wait.

Second, rising prices across all premium smartphones have led to consumers being willing to pay higher prices than would previously have been the case. Apple has absorbed some of the increased component costs, making the iPhone 18 Pro comparatively better value.

Third is what Counterpoint describes as “aggressive channel support,” generally meaning heavy advertising and promotions by retailers and carriers.

title: Pixel Recorder makes it easier to access audio files
snippet: Pixel Recorder is getting a small quality-of-life update that surfaces your audio files to other apps on your device. more…
fullText:
Pixel Recorder is getting a small quality-of-life update that surfaces your audio files to other apps on your device.

Previously, accessing the actual audio file involved opening a recording and then the share menu for the “Audio or transcript file” option. This took you to the system share sheet for a manual save. 

Pixel Recorder now has an “Access recordings in other apps” setting that lets you “View your recordings in the Files app or other apps for easier access.” 

This is enabled by default, with a prompt on the homepage announcing the new feature: “Access recordings in other apps. Manage this in Settings anytime.”

	

The new “Recordings” folder on your device shows all audio that you’ve recorded or downloaded from the cloud.

Version 4.2.20260823.x of Pixel Recorder widely rolls out this capability.

It follows the last update in August that introduced the new app icon, which is not yet live (along with Weather) on the Pixel Watch. Recorder will also be available on Googlebooks going forward.

title: Spotify billionaire’s body scan startup has come to America
snippet: Farooq Abbasi, an investor in Neko Health, talked to Equity about the hot health tech company and what's next for it.
fullText:
Neko Health seems to be the hottest body scan in the world right now. 

The scan, co-founded by Spotify’s David Ek and Hjalmar Nilsonne, uses advanced technology to screen for issues in the blood, skin, and metabolism. The company was founded in Sweden, has raised nearly $1 billion total, and just landed in New York. It has a global waitlist already topping 300,000 people, the company says.

TechCrunch sat down with Farooq Abbasi of Preface Ventures, who invested in the company. He hopes Neko Health can be the future of preventative medicine, especially in a country like the United States, where the medical system is notoriously plagued with issues. 

Abbasi contends that preventative care utilization is low in the U.S. as people have concerns about how much it costs. Currently, Neko Health charges $500 for its one-hour scan, which is not covered by insurance but should qualify as an acceptable expense for those that have health savings accounts (HSAs). “I think preventative care and healthcare should be cheap and accessible,” Abbasi said. 

The hope is that Neko Health can tackle some of these issues, and it’s currently eyeing an expansion across the U.S. Abbasi has been scanned twice already and, perhaps, no surprise, says he loves it. “I think there should be Neko clinics everywhere,” he said. 

He says the product has grown so much since he first tried it. “In my generation one scan, it was a blood test with 15 biomarkers,” he said. “It was fifty-five this time.” 

Neko also uses advanced computer vision for its scans and Abbasi sees this as another example of how AI is improving the medical sector overall. He argues that Neko Health isn’t just another wellness fad, but something that gives people “actionable insights to make their lives better,” he said. 

Neko still has a long way to go in the U.S., especially on scaling and regulatory approval. But Abbasi is an optimist; he hopes more venture dollars will pour into the right companies and doesn’t think anything is too broken to fix.

title: Google Wallet for Android adds 12th digital state ID
snippet: Following the last launch at the end of August, Google Wallet is rolling out support for Oklahoma state IDs on Android. more…
fullText:
Following the last launch at the end of August, Google Wallet is rolling out support for Oklahoma state IDs on Android.

Open Google Wallet on your phone and tap the ‘plus’ button next to “View more” at the bottom > IDs & personal info > Driver’s license or state ID. This reveals Oklahoma as the 13th Google Wallet option. It joins Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Georgia, Iowa, Maryland, Montana, New Mexico, North Dakota, Ohio, and Puerto Rico.

The card design shows the American Bison (state animal) and the scissor-tailed flycatcher (state bird).

The set-up process requires taking photos of the front and back of your physical card, as well as a short video of your face for verification that gets sent to the SOK. This review can take a few minutes with a notification confirming once it’s available. You’ll also get an email confirmation from the state agency.

	

First, tap on the reader or scan your QR code: Your personal info won’t be shared yet. On your phone, review what info you want to share.

Next, review what info will be shared: Make sure you’re comfortable sharing the info they request

You don’t need to hand your phone to anyone: Your ID will be securely shared using Bluetooth, so make sure it’s on

Lastly, verify it’s you to share your info: For extra security, verify that this ID is yours using your face, fingerprint, password, or PIN

“Details” next to “Show code” lets you enable an “Activity history,” while “Driver’s License information” lists license number, date of expiry, address, and more.

IDs can be read via NFC or by having the QR code scanned. It is accepted at some airports by the TSA. Officially, you still have to carry your ID card as the one on your phone “does not replace the requirement for individuals to carry a physical card.” 

Your device must be running Android 8+ and have a screen lock, with Bluetooth and Nearby devices enabled. A state ID can be deleted from Google Wallet at any time or remotely via myaccount.google.com. As a private pass, it does not get synced to the cloud and is only available on one device.

Tap Personal Info.

Scroll to “Digital ID.”

Tap Manage Digital ID.

Next to the ID or license that you want to remove, tap Delete.

Confirm that you want to delete your ID from your device and Google Account.

snippet: There’s very little left of the Galaxy S27 Ultra left to surface before launch, but new information might change what to expect in Samsung’s device color options. more…
fullText:
There’s very little left of the Galaxy S27 Ultra left to surface before launch, but new information might change what to expect in Samsung’s device color options.

According to a short and straightforward post on Twitter/X by @UniverseIce, the Galaxy S27 Ultra series will come in four base color variants – Black, Blue, Light Pink, and White. That doesn’t include the Samsung online exclusive colorways, which usually add a couple of hues to the lineup.

Previous leaks claimed Samsung would offer the Galaxy S27 Ultra in five colors, all of the above included except Purple. It’s unclear whether a purple version was excluded this time around, or if Samsung plans to sell the version as an online-exclusive. Those don’t cost more, but they’re only available from the company’s website and not third-party retailers.

It would be a first in four years if Samsung didn’t release a purple Galaxy S Ultra phone. The Galaxy S23 Ultra in 2023 came in Lavender, and since then, every Galaxy S Ultra phone has been available in some similar shade.

	

It’s worth a quick note that Light Pink comes so very close to Lavender on the color wheel, so do with that information what you will.

In combination with the new camera bar, the Galaxy S27 Ultra will take on an entirely new look. Its design is set rather far from the look of nearly every Galaxy S Ultra phone since 2021, thanks to the camera island spanning the entire rear panel.

Whether you like it or not, the Galaxy S27 Ultra will look like an entirely different phone. And now, it will look different in LavenderLight Pink.

Of course, that hinges on whether the leaks we’ve seen prove true. Samsung plans to launch the new devices early next year.

title: Fantastical’s long-awaited Android debut begins today on Googlebook
snippet: Fantastical has long been hailed as one of the greatest calendar apps available today, but if you’re an Android user, there’s a good chance you’ve never used it. Despite a move from Apple exclusivity to cross-platform availability on Windows, Android has long eluded the attention of development team Flexibits. Today, that’s finally changing, as Fantastical is headed to Google’s mobile OS platform — but not precisely in the way you might expect. more…
fullText:
Fantastical has long been hailed as one of the greatest calendar apps available today, but if you’re an Android user, there’s a good chance you’ve never used it. Despite a move from Apple exclusivity to cross-platform availability on Windows, Android has long eluded the attention of development team Flexibits. Today, that’s finally changing, as Fantastical is headed to Google’s mobile OS platform — but not precisely in the way you might expect.

Beginning today, Fantastical is now available for Google’s new laptop initiative, Googlebook. Existing Fantastical users who rely on the app on different platforms (like iOS or Windows) can access Fantastical on Googlebook at no additional charge, while new users coming to Fantastical for the very first time can likewise also use the application on any of their other supported devices.

While the underlying OS on Googlebook is Android, Flexibits’ co-founder and CEO Michael Simmons stressed that the application isn’t quite ready yet to debut on phones, tablets, or foldables. Those versions are on the way — bucking what Simmons himself said back in 2024 when he declared the app would never find its way to the Play Store — but they won’t be ready for launch until sometime in 2027. Likewise, today’s announcement does not include bringing the company’s contact management app, Cardhop, to Android; Simmons tells me they have “no announcement” about that app at this time.

Fantastical began life on Mac back in 2011, offering calendar creation tools via a straightforward ordinary language-based interface that isn’t all too dissimilar to today’s LLMs. Though Flexibits unveiled a Windows variant in late 2024, today’s move marks the first step towards compatibility with Google’s mobile OS, and you can thank Googlebooks for building that bridge. Simmons told me development began after Google showed the Fantastical team a demo of its new laptop platform, and he found himself impressed enough to take a chance on finally expanding the app to Android.

	

While most users will have to wait until next year to get their hands on Fantastical, all you early Googlebook adopters out there have the chance to begin using a brand-new calendar app starting today. Individual pricing starts at $57 per year, with family plans starting at $90 annually. A free, less powerful tier is also available.

title: Why the Moon Is a Legal Wild West
snippet: Private companies are taking cremated remains and stunt payloads to the moon. Former NASA attorney Steve Mirmina warns that there’s nothing stopping them.
fullText:
For $3,495, you can send your pet’s ashes to the moon. 

Celestis calls itself “the most compelling pet memorial service on or off the planet,” allowing customers to send a “symbolic portion” of their pet’s ashes to live forever on the lunar surface. (Prices are the same for human remains, Celestis says.) It’s part of a growing wave of companies looking to capitalize on the regulatory gray area that the moon inhabits. 

A Japanese beverage company sent up a payload that looked like one of its Pocari Sweat energy drinks in 2014. Artist Jeff Koons sent up 125 mini-sculptures in 2024; each one corresponded to an NFT that collectors could purchase back on Earth. One man has even raised $227,000 to put a giant cross on the moon. All told, humans have left nearly 500,000 pounds of stuff on the moon’s surface to date, most of which consists of government-sent lunar landers, surveyors and other dead spacecraft.

			

More from CNET

This explosion of commercial lunar activity is technically legal, says Steve Mirmina, a professor of space law at Georgetown University and former NASA attorney. 

“I searched and searched the law, and unfortunately, there’s no law against launching race cars,” he said, referring to Elon Musk’s launching of a Tesla Roadster in 2018. “We don’t have a government agency with the legal authority to regulate what happens on the moon.”

Existing US law doesn’t sufficiently regulate what we actually send to the lunar surface, Mirmina argues in Lawful but Awful: U.S. Regulation of Commercial Activities on the Lunar Surface, published Sept. 19 in Air and Space Law. Without a more sustainable legal framework, we risk turning the moon into “Earth’s junk drawer.” 

Who regulates the moon?

To date, 118 countries are parties to the Outer Space Treaty, which was originally enacted in 1967 during the height of the Cold War. It stipulates that space is free for use by all countries, and that they have a duty to avoid harmful contamination in space. 

The 2020 Artemis Accords further enshrined norms of space sustainability into international law. While not legally binding, it constitutes “soft law” norms that shape best practices in space. 

Countries are left to enforce compliance on the private space companies within their borders. In the US, the Federal Aviation Administration governs rocket launches, and NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services program partners with American companies to deliver payloads to the moon. But Congress hasn’t given any one agency the authority to regulate what private companies are actually putting on those payloads. 

“It’s not very useful that they can regulate launch if they can’t regulate what happens after the rocket’s in space,” said Mirmina. “Basically, NASA, the FAA, even the State Department – they’re all kind of pointing at each other, hoping somebody did something. And then nobody had the legal authority to do anything.”

Real-world costs of unchecked commercialization

No one wants to gaze up at the night sky and see an energy drink advertisement. None of this activity has affected our view of the moon so far, and most of it falls into the “annoying” category more than the “truly reprehensible.” But Mirmina worries that there’s no legal safeguard in place to halt some truly awful conduct. 

What’s happening on the moon right now has already stirred outrage from a number of different groups. Navajo Nation President Buu Nygren wrote a letter to NASA in 2023 asking the agency to stop sending human remains to the moon.

“It is crucial to emphasize that the Moon holds a sacred position in many Indigenous cultures, including ours,” Nygren wrote. “The act of depositing human remains and other materials, which could be perceived as discards in any other location, on the moon is tantamount to desecration of this sacred space.”

There’s also the question of how to be good caretakers for future generations. Moon landings produce something called “plume–surface interactions,” in which exhaust from descending spacecraft kicks up rocks and dust at speeds faster than a bullet. When new payloads land with increasing frequency, yesterday’s pet ashes or energy drink advertisements could become tomorrow’s projectiles. Unlike on Earth, the moon has a very thin atmosphere with little erosion, so every item placed on the surface stays “forever,” as Celestis promises customers.

“They become shrapnel for future lunar missions,” Mirmina says. “It’s just a lot easier to prevent it than it’s going to ever be to try to clean it up.”

Stewardship before it’s too late

Everything is hard in space, especially agreeing on the right way to behave in a domain that seems so distant and invulnerable. But it’s also one corner of the government with rare bipartisan approval: Roughly three-quarters of Americans have a favorable opinion of NASA, and seven in 10 say it is essential that the US continue to be a world leader in space, according to the Pew Research Center. Most also support NASA’s goal of sending astronauts back to the moon in 2028.

“Before we’ve really even explored the moon, we’re already tossing up junk to live on there forever,” Mirmina says. “If you care about space or stewardship or the environment, we should preserve it for future explorers and not ruin it before they get there.”

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Joe Supan
						

						

							Senior Writer						
					

											

								

											Joe Supan is a senior writer for CNET covering home technology, broadband, and moving. Prior to joining CNET, Joe led MyMove's moving coverage and reported on broadband policy, the digital divide, and privacy issues for the broadband marketplace Allconnect. He has been featured as a guest columnist on Broadband Breakfast, and his work has been referenced by the Los Angeles Times, Forbes, National Geographic, Yahoo! Finance and more.

For $3,495, you can send your pet’s ashes to the moon.

Celestis calls itself “the most compelling pet memorial service on or off the planet,” allowing customers to send a “symbolic portion” of their pet’s ashes to live forever on the lunar surface. (Prices are the same for human remains, Celestis says.) It’s part of a growing wave of companies looking to capitalize on the regulatory gray area that the moon inhabits.

title: Elder fraud is rising – here’s how to protect your family
snippet: Elder fraud – where seniors are deliberately targeted due to this demographic having lower rates of tech literacy – is becoming a growing problem in the US. According to Incogni’s analysis of FBI data, 72% of elder fraud cases in 2024 were enabled by victims’ personal data being exposed online, accounting for $4.2 billion in losses. more…
fullText:
Elder fraud – where seniors are deliberately targeted due to this demographic having lower rates of tech literacy – is becoming a growing problem in the US.

According to Incogni’s analysis of FBI data, 72% of elder fraud cases in 2024 were enabled by victims’ personal data being exposed online, accounting for $4.2 billion in losses.

How these scams work

Family chat groups can be a goldmine for scammers. Everyday updates ranging from doctor visits to travel plans provide personalized information scammers can use to make it much easier to convincingly impersonate family members in trouble.

Given that iMessage, WhatsApp, and most other messaging apps use end-to-end encryption, you might assume this information is completely safe, but that isn’t always true. One of the most dangerous tools employed by scammers is what’s known as SIM swaps.

With this, they’ll use whatever personal information they can find from public sources in order to convince a mobile carrier that they are the person they are targeting. They claim the phone has been lost or damaged and ask the carrier to switch the mobile number to a new SIM card they have purchased.

If the carrier is fooled, then all texts sent to the victim will instead be received by the scammer. This includes SMS-based two-factor authentication codes to reset passwords, access bank accounts, and more. It is this capability that can give the scammer access to family chat groups.

The combination of the personal data they’ve already found online with the additional details they can glean from the chats gives them everything they need to convincingly persuade their victim that they are a family member in need of urgent assistance. This includes voice notes providing the audio required to create deepfake speech that appears to be the voice of the family member.

How to protect your family

There are three main steps you can take to protect your family members against this type of attack.

First, minimize the personal data a scammer can find online. Scammers use data broker sites to obtain information like family names and phone numbers, as well as information like hobbies and travel history. There are literally hundreds of different data brokers, and getting personal data removed from all of them is a mammoth task. Fortunately, Incogni can do it for you.

Second, ensure that two-factor authentication (2FA) is switched on for all messaging apps, social media, and more. The bottom line is that any time you are offered the opportunity to use 2FA, you should accept it. If you’re offered the choice between text message and authenticator app to receive the codes, always choose the app. This is your best protection against SIM swap attacks.

Third, always contact the family member by a different method in order to verify that it really is them. If you get a text message, for example, then email them in response. If you get an email, then phone them. The more communications channels a scammer has to compromise, the lower the chance of them succeeding.

Finally, agree a secret family password which will be used to verify identity during emergency calls. If you receive a call claiming to be a family member in need of urgent assistance, always ask them for the password, even if you think you recognize their voice and they know seem to know lots of personal things. This is the final layer of protection against a scammer who has access to a family member’s phone number, email account, and more.

fullText:
10 years ago today, Google launched the first Pixel smartphone and, at the time, teased it by saying we’d still be talking about it years later. And, yeah, we still are, and this is a Google project that shows no signs of slowing down.

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every Sunday along with ‘Inbox’ on Tuesday and Thursday. You can find past issues here.

Google has a bit of a reputation for churning through projects. If something isn’t a hit, it either gets canned or converted into something else. And that’s what many assumed would happen to Pixel, especially during the lean years in the middle of the series. While Pixel hit the ground running with great first impressions, missteps on the Pixel 2 XL’s display, the Pixel 3 XL’s funky bathtub notch, and the Pixel 4 series just, as a whole, left room for plenty of doubt.

Prior to the first Pixel’s launch, Google’s at-the-time head of Android, Hiroshi Lockheimer, said that we’d still “be talking about October 4, 2016.” And, 10 years later, he wasn’t wrong. 

	

Google has stuck to its guns around Pixel, and perhaps expanded the project more than anyone might have thought. Investments like a mid-range lineup, Tensor chips, and a whole ecosystem of accessories weren’t really in the thought process a decade ago. Yet, here we are. 

We’ve revisited several of Google’s Pixel devices this week and asked our readers what they think the best Pixel of all time is. So far, Pixel 10 Pro XL is winning that poll.

title: DoorDash now lets you order by text in Apple Messages
snippet: DoorDash today launched a new way to order your next meal: via text in Apple’s Messages app, powered by AI. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
DoorDash today launched a new way to order your next meal: via text in Apple’s Messages app, powered by AI. Here are the details.

DoorDash text ordering launches on iPhone, powered by AI agent

AI agents are here to stay, and they don’t just look like cute digital creatures. While Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots have gotten a lot of attention, AI agents are popping up in ways that are less obviously “AI” too.

For example, today DoorDash launched the ability to skip the app and simply text to place your food order in Apple’s Messages app. It’s available in the US only to start, and interested users will need to first join this waitlist. And it’s all powered by an AI agent.

Here’s the rundown on how it works, via DoorDash’s announcement:

Text what you’re craving: Ask for a specific dish, request a local recommendation based on your mood, or simply reorder your go-to Friday night meal for the family.

Skip the search: DoorDash searches local spots, scans menus, and suggests a cart based on what you’re in the mood for. It even texts you photos of the food it recommends right from the restaurant’s store page on the DoorDash app. 

Truly personalized ordering: Text “order my usual” and it knows you mean your Friday night order — no need to spell out the dish, the modifiers, or the restaurant. It already knows whether you skip cilantro, always add extra sauce, or never miss dessert. The more you order, the more it learns, and if you want, it can message you proactively to ask if you want your usual coffee order based on your daily habits.

Manage group preferences with ease: Ordering for large groups is never easy, especially when everyone wants something different. It can handle mixed dietary preferences and different quantities in one order, so you’re not the one juggling everyone’s requests.

Checkout without ever opening the app: Confirm your order right inside the text thread and it manages checkout.

To get started, join DoorDash’s waitlist and you’ll be notified when text access is granted. Depending on demand, that access might arrive right away, or it may take some time.

Are you interested in using DoorDash’s AI agent to order via Apple’s Messages app? Let us know in the comments.
