title: Google’s original Pixel Fold was the right idea years ahead of its time
snippet: Google’s original Pixel Fold was inherently flawed but also fundamentally way better than I expected and, thanks to recent arrivals, also way ahead of its time. more…
fullText:
Google’s original Pixel Fold was inherently flawed but also fundamentally way better than I expected and, thanks to recent arrivals, also way ahead of its time.

Foldables were still very much going through growing pains in 2023 when Google stepped up to the plate with its first foldable, the Pixel Fold. At the time, I called it “better than it should be, but far from perfect,” and I stand by that. Even with hindsight of three more Google foldables and the rapid improvements of the rest of the industry, the Pixel Fold managed to do a lot right at the time. It offered sturdy hardware, respectable cameras, and less compromises than most other foldables of the time.

Has it aged well? Not particularly. The glossy finish to the metal frame remains a fingerprint magnet in the worst kind of way, and the sheer heft of this phone is wild. I don’t often take issue with a heavy smartphone, but especially compared to the Galaxy Z Fold 8 I’ve been using the past couple of months, the original Pixel Fold is noticeably heavy in the hand. The crease down the center is huge, and it’s a thick device too. And, three years later, I can only imagine how bad Tensor G2’s heat management issues have become – that was ultimately the deal-breaker for me when I was using the device last. 

Yet, for everything it got wrong, the Pixel Fold got one thing right, the form factor.

	

In the wake of Apple’s debut in the foldable market, brands are quickly pivoting to wider form factors, and they seem to be resonating with customers. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is a smash hit, and I bet we’ll be seeing a lot more of these wide foldables over the next year. 

But the Pixel Fold did it three years ago, albeit with a lot less flash. 

Google’s foldable looks almost normal compared to a Galaxy Z Fold 8, but the core idea is the same. The wider canvas is designed for better multitasking and tablet apps, something that I pointed out in my original review. Where Samsung’s foldables were really good at using phone apps on a bigger canvas, the Pixel Fold was far more likely to trigger a proper tablet version of an app instead. 

	

Google ultimately threw that away. Why? Android apps simply weren’t ready at the time. While Android apps have always been designed around scaling to form factors, bigger and wider canvases were still in the minority, and most apps didn’t fully support them. As such, the taller and squarish design just made more sense.

Arguably, it still does, but Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 has shown that it works when you do it “right.” Two months into using it, I’m thrilled with this form factor, and a bit annoyed that Google gave up on it so quickly even though, at the time, it probably made sense. Unfortunately, that’s a bit of a trend in the Pixel’s legacy and Google’s as a whole – Inbox, Stadia, etc. It doesn’t take much to find a Google idea that was left behind too quickly.

It’s anyone’s guess when Google might revisit this design, but I hope it happens.

title: AT&T claims iOS 27.0.1 fixes iPhone 18 Pro Max cellular issues, but users disagree [U]

In a new text message to customers, AT&T says affected users should update their devices to iOS 26.0.1 to fix the issues … but early reports indicate the update doesn’t actually fix the problem. more…
fullText:
Update 1:50 p.m. PT: More details from Apple are available here: 

Apple confirms iPhone 18 Pro Max AT&T cellular issues, affected devices require hardware replacement

Since the iPhone 18 Pro Max launched, some AT&T customers have complained of various connectivity issues.

In a new text message to customers, AT&T says affected users should update their devices to iOS 26.0.1 to fix the issues … but early reports indicate the update doesn’t actually fix the problem.

AT&T tells iPhone 18 Pro Max users to install iOS 27.0.1 

In a thread on Reddit today, an AT&T customer says they received the following automated text message from the carrier:

Hi, it’s AT&T. Action needed: An important Apple software update for your iPhone 18 Pro Max is available. Some phones may be unable to complete calls/text/data, including to 911. Update to iOS 27.0.1 immediately — Settings > General > Software Update. Please contact AT&T or Apple if you have questions.

Apple released iOS 27.0.1 earlier this week. According to the release notes, the update addressed bugs related to Face ID and camera performance for iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max users. The release notes made no mention of any fixes for cellular connectivity problems impacting AT&T customers.

Early reports from AT&T users suggest that iOS 27.0.1 does not fix the connectivity problems affecting iPhone 18 Pro Max. Many affected users say they updated when iOS 27.0.1 was released on Monday and are still facing the same problems.

Affected iPhone 18 Pro Max users can’t connect to AT&T’s network for calls, texts, and data. The users see “SOS” in their iPhone’s status bar. The connectivity issues aren’t impacting every iPhone 18 Pro Max user, but they do appear to be relatively widespread.

Interestingly, the problems appear to be exclusive to the iPhone 18 Pro Max, which uses a Qualcomm modem. The iPhone 18 Pro, which uses Apple’s C2 modem, is seemingly unaffected by these AT&T connectivity issues.

Are you an iPhone 18 Pro Max user facing connectivity issues with AT&T? Does iOS 27.0.1 fix the problems? Let us know down in the comments.

Update 10:50 a.m. PT: In a statement to MacRumors, AT&T emphasized that affected iPhone 18 Pro Max users should update to iOS 27.0.1. The carrier added that it’s working with Apple to solve the problems. Apple also released an AT&T carrier settings update today.

title: Gemini app starts rolling out big side panel simplification, settings redesign
snippet: The next big update to the Gemini app on Android and iOS is beginning to roll out with a focus on simplifying core navigation. more…
fullText:
The next big update to the Gemini app on Android and iOS is beginning to roll out with a focus on simplifying core navigation.

There are no major changes to the homepage, with the first differences found in the side panel. Search has moved to the top-right corner, while the chat history now offers filters: All, Ready, Needs attention, and In progress.

“Scheduled” is a new item in the list and replaces the “Scheduled actions” page. You get “Suggested” prompts like Create a news digest or Build a study quiz.

“Customize” is the big update today. The “Discover” tab surfaces skills, which are replacing Gems, and third-party connected apps. Notably, skills are activated using the ‘@’ symbol instead of a forward slash like in Gemini Spark. This page feels like a mini-app store for Gemini.

	

Meanwhile, the “Connectors” tab serves as a modernized “Connected Apps” page. Gemini is leaning into that app store parlance with the ability to “Uninstall” from the overflow menu.

Meanwhile, Gemini is getting a much-needed Settings redesign when you tap your profile avatar in the top-right corner or the gear icon. Manage account and Usage limits make up the first grouping, followed by:

Preferences: Notifications, Personal Intelligence, Avatar, Gem manager, Theme, Voice, Media, Device controls, Gemini Notebook

Data & privacy: Import memory, Contact info from your devices, Gemini Apps Activity, Your public links, Privacy Help Hub

Support: Help, Report a problem, About, Updates 

This redesign is not yet widely rolled out and only appearing on one of our Google Accounts. That said, it’s appearing on both Android and iOS.

title: Jack Dorsey’s Bitchat disappears from app stores in India after government order
snippet: Bitchat has become largely unavailable in India as a result of the restrictions.
fullText:
Bitchat, Jack Dorsey’s decentralized messaging app designed to work without an internet connection, has disappeared from Apple and Google app stores in India, months after New Delhi first sought to restrict access to the open source software.

Dorsey said Saturday that the Indian government had ordered Apple to remove Bitchat from its App Store in the country. In a notice from Apple that Dorsey posted on X, India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued the demand under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, the country’s primary legal provision for government-ordered online blocking.

Apple’s notice said Bitchat would remain available on its App Store outside India. However, access to the app through its TestFlight beta-testing service would also be blocked in the country.

Bitchat was also no longer available for download through Google Play in India when TechCrunch checked on Saturday. Bitchat’s website was also inaccessible across various internet service providers in the country. It was not immediately clear whether Google and internet service providers had also received directions from the federal government.

Apple, Google, and India’s IT ministry did not respond to requests for comment.

Launched in July last year, Bitchat uses Bluetooth mesh networking to allow nearby devices to exchange encrypted messages without relying on cellular networks, internet access, or centralized servers.

In July 2026, Dorsey revealed that Indian authorities had ordered GitHub to take down repositories associated with the open source messaging app, raising questions among digital rights advocates and legal experts about the legal basis for restricting software based on its functionality.

The Indian government said in its order to GitHub at the time that Bitchat’s architecture made it hard for law enforcement agencies to intercept communications or trace users, and pointed to its ability to continue operating during internet shutdowns. The July order relied on a provision of India’s information technology law that deals with intermediaries and their liability for third-party content. That differs from Section 69A, cited in Apple’s latest notice.

The Internet Freedom Foundation, a New Delhi-based digital rights advocacy group, called the latest order unconstitutional, arguing that Section 69A allows the government to block unlawful information but not a messaging app because of its ability to operate during internet shutdowns. It also said neither the blocking order nor the allegedly illegal content cited as the basis for the action had been made public.

The latest restrictions on Bitchat come as India is seeing a fresh wave of ⁠youth-led protests over changes to the country’s voter rolls. Police detained several people during demonstrations in New Delhi on Saturday, as protesters demanded the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner over alleged manipulation of electoral rolls. Authorities suspended internet services around New Delhi’s Jantar Mantar for 12 hours on Friday during protests there.

During July’s protests, demonstrators reportedly turned to Bitchat and rival app Briar after authorities suspended internet services.

Interest in Bitchat surged in India around the same time. The country accounted for about 85% of the app’s global downloads between July 17 and July 23, up from roughly 1% in the previous 30 days, data from market intelligence firm Sensor Tower showed.

title: Google details Gems to skills migration, including free access
snippet: As we spotted over the weekend, Gemini is replacing Gems with skills, and Google today fully detailed the migration. more…
fullText:
As we spotted over the weekend, Gemini is replacing Gems with skills, and Google today fully detailed the migration.

The news today is that skills are now available in the Gemini chat experience after debuting in the Spark agent. These reusable instructions for common tasks can be invoked with a / command from the main prompt box instead of having to launch via the Gem manager. This offers a more unified experience in the long run.

Example skills include preparing for presentations, matching writing styles, and getting different perspectives.

Skills will gain feature parity with Gems over the coming weeks. This includes the ability to share skills with others using links, and adding Google Drive files or notebooks for context. 

	

Gemini will automatically migrate Gems to skills, with the new feature available for all free users who don’t have Spark. 

Personal Google Accounts will lose access to Gems starting in November. The migration will happen for Google Workspace business, enterprise, and non-profit customers in March 2027, while education users have until June 2027.

Skills start rolling out today to Gemini chat users globally. All other customers can expect access in the coming weeks.

title: Gemini for Android Auto is just giving up on answers for some drivers
snippet: The promise of Gemini for Android Auto is huge, as the AI assistant is theoretically more capable than Assistant was. But, as it’s now becoming the only option, a weird issue is leaving Gemini for Android Auto perhaps less than useless, as it just gives up on answers from drivers. more…
fullText:
The promise of Gemini for Android Auto is huge, as the AI assistant is theoretically more capable than Assistant was. But, as it’s now becoming the only option, a weird issue is leaving Gemini for Android Auto perhaps less than useless, as it just gives up on answers from drivers.

To say Gemini’s launch on Android Auto has been riddled with issues is a bit of an understatement. For months users have reported problems with various commands and just overlooked bits of functionality. I’m personally still waiting on Google to fix the issue where Gemini just keeps on talking or waiting for a response after I’ve completed a task via the touchscreen instead.

A new issue popped up this week, though, that’s not only frustrating, but just a waste of time.

Users report that Gemini for Android Auto is hearing commands, processing them, and then just giving up entirely on the answer. A Reddit user shared a video of this and several others chimed in with the same problem, and it’s one I’ve also personally encountered just this week. 

	

	

The issue doesn’t seem to have anything to do with signal strength or the question being asked. Gemini just sits there thinking for a few moments before giving up.

The video above demonstrates the issue when paired to a Pixel phone, but users report the same issue when paired to Samsung and Motorola devices too; I’ve noticed it with my Galaxy Z Fold 8. Google has, so far, not acknowledged the problem as far as we’ve been able to find.

Are you running into this problem?

title: Watch F1 on Apple TV tonight, free for everyone in the US
snippet: The Bahrain Grand Prix is streaming for free on Apple TV this weekend, subscription not required. Rather amusingly, the location of the Bahrain Grand Prix is actually in Sepang, Malaysia. Usually, F1 on Apple TV requires a paid subscription. But this weekend, it’s free for everyone to tune in. You can catch up on qualifying in preparation to stream the live race tonight, which kicks off at 3 AM Eastern Time. more…
fullText:
The Bahrain Grand Prix is streaming for free on Apple TV this weekend, subscription not required. Rather amusingly, the location of the Bahrain Grand Prix is actually in Sepang, Malaysia. 

Usually, F1 on Apple TV requires a paid subscription. But this weekend, it’s free for everyone to tune in. You can catch up on qualifying in preparation to stream the live race tonight, which kicks off at 3 AM Eastern Time.

All you need to watch is to get the Apple TV app on a compatible device, be in the United States, and stay up late enough to watch live. 

Coverage starts at 1:50 AM Eastern Time, with the race scheduled to start at 3 AM Eastern Time. You can of course watch later on-demand, if you’d opt to go to bed at a reasonable hour. 

You can get the Apple TV app on Apple devices, Amazon Fire Stick, Roku, PlayStation, Xbox, Android and more. You can also watch in a web browser at tv.apple.com. 

With qualifying happening earlier today, Red Bull’s Max Verstappen has snatched pole position for the first time this season, with Lewis Hamilton taking second and championship leader Kim Antonelli in third. It’s Red Bull’s best chance at a race win so far this year.

You may be wondering why the Bahrain Grand Prix is being hosted in Malaysia. In a normal year, the Bahrain GP would have happened much earlier in the season. But due to the ongoing Iran war, the race was cancelled and the Bahrain organizers instead decided to sponsor a race elsewhere in the world instead. 

Despite not being part of the official F1 calendar anymore, Sepang is a fan favourite circuit that should make for some exciting action on track. 

Again, use the Apple TV app to tune in for free, no subscription required. The race starts at 3 AM Eastern Time, with broadcast coverage starting at 1:50 AM.

title: Google Home now lets you preview Nest Doorbell ringtones, just in time for the holidays
snippet: Smart doorbells usually center their features around their security features — person alerts, motion tracking, the works — but they also go a long way in making your front door a little more fun. Google is no stranger to seasonal doorbell chimes, and ahead of a few months packed with holidays, the company is making a big improvement to how you setup your doorbell ringtones. more…
fullText:
Smart doorbells usually center their features around their security features — person alerts, motion tracking, the works — but they also go a long way in making your front door a little more fun. Google is no stranger to seasonal doorbell chimes, and ahead of a few months packed with holidays, the company is making a big improvement to how you setup your doorbell ringtones.

As part of today’s Google Home update, you can finally preview the chime you’re assigning to your Nest Doorbell from within the app itself, saving you the hassle of having to stand in front of your own door to hear it for yourself. Home now includes audio previews for both standard chimes and limited-time holiday themes, making it easy to know exactly what spooky sound — or Christmas jingle — your visitors will hear whenever they arrive.

Unfortunately, you’ll still need to wait for those timed offerings to be available throughout the year; only Oktoberfest is currently actively available under Google’s doorbell theme settings. Still, our own Ben Schoon is already seeing the play button active and available within the Home app for both seasonal and classic themes, with a play button available to the left of every option.

You can find this option within the Doorbell theme menu under Doorbell camera settings in the Google Home app. If you’re anxiously awaiting some Halloween tones as October rolls in, however, you’ll need to keep waiting. Meanwhile, the Oktoberfest sound ends its annual run on October 9th.

fullText:
Thousands of startups applied. Just 200 made Startup Battlefield. Only 20 will pitch on the Disrupt Stage across all three days. Competition goes from October 13-15 at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026. It all comes down to one final decision.

For our Startup Battlefield finalist judges, we set a particularly high bar: Each has founded or co-founded the investment firm they now lead. They know what separates a great pitch from a potentially great company — and they’ll be the five people deciding who becomes this year’s Startup Battlefield champion.

And the conversation won’t end with the final pitch. Later that afternoon, all five judges will reunite on the Builders Stage for a live AMA, where the audience can ask them anything — from what stood out in the competition and what they look for in founders to fundraising, company building, and where they’re looking to invest next.

Grab your pass now and save up to $100 and get a second pass at 50% off. Or bring a group of four or more, saving up to 30%.

Meet the five investors who will decide this year’s Startup Battlefield winner

Image Credits:TechCrunch

Stacy Brown-Philpot, Founder and Managing Partner, Cherryrock Capital

Stacy Brown-Philpot is the founder and managing partner of Cherryrock Capital, a venture fund focused on Series A and Series B software companies built by Black and Latinx founders. Her portfolio includes Coactive AI, a multimodal AI platform for media and entertainment, and Vitable Health, which provides primary care plans for hourly workers. Brown-Philpot previously served as CEO of TaskRabbit, which was acquired by IKEA, and spent more than a decade in senior roles at Google. She holds an MBA from Stanford University.

Chi-Hua Chien, Co-Founder and Managing Partner, Goodwater Capital

Chi-Hua Chien is a co-founder and managing partner of Goodwater Capital, where he invests exclusively in consumer technology — including mobile, fintech, e-commerce, digital health, and consumer AI — across the United States and Asia. With more than 17 unicorns backed across his career, his portfolio includes Spotify, Chime, Monzo, TikTok/Musical.ly, Coupang, Toss, and Udemy. Before co-founding Goodwater, Chien was a general partner at Kleiner Perkins and a principal at Accel.

Dayna Grayson, Co-Founder and General Partner, Construct Capital

Dayna Grayson is a co-founder and general partner at Construct Capital, a Washington, D.C.-based early-stage fund focused on technology for foundational American industries, including manufacturing, logistics, transportation, supply chain, and defense. Her portfolio includes Veho, Hadrian, Copia Automation, Arkestro, and Verve Motion. Before co-founding Construct, Grayson was a partner at NEA, where she led early investments, including Desktop Metal, which went public on the NYSE. She holds a degree in systems engineering from the University of Virginia and an MBA from Harvard Business School.

Image Credits:Haje Kamps

Carter Reum, Co-Founder and Managing Partner, M13

Carter Reum is a co-founder and managing partner of M13, a consumer technology venture firm with $1.9 billion under management that invests in seed to Series B companies shaping the future of work, commerce, health, and money. Across more than 200 investments, M13 has backed companies such as Lyft, Pinterest, Ring, Daily Harvest, and Tonal — with 15 unicorns in the portfolio. Before launching M13, Reum co-founded VEEV Spirit, one of the fastest-growing independent spirits brands in the country, which was acquired in 2016. He is co-author of the national bestseller “Shortcut Your Startup” and holds a BA from Columbia University.

Alexa on Tobel, Founder and Managing Partner, Inspired Capital

Alexa Von Tobel is the founder and managing partner of Inspired Capital, which she co-founded with former U.S. Secretary of Commerce Penny Pritzker. Her portfolio includes MosaicML, acquired by Databricks, as well as Chief, Finix, and Dandy — with nine unicorns backed across her investing career. Before launching Inspired Capital, Von Tobel founded LearnVest, a financial planning platform acquired by Northwestern Mutual. She is a New York Times bestselling author and a certified financial planner.

title: TCL’s paperlike OLED phone made me more excited for the iPhone Duo
snippet: TCL’s P80 Ultra is its first Nxtpaper phone with an OLED screen. | Photo: Dominic Preston / The Verge I've spent most of the last couple weeks using an otherwise unexceptional midrange Android phone with one amazing feature: a matte OLED display. That screen is by far the best thing about the TCL P80 Ultra, and weirdly, it's made me more excited for the iPhone Duo and its matte inner display. 2023's TCL Nxtpaper 40 first brought matte displays to the company's phones after they appeared on tablets in 2021. Nxtpaper is more than a simple matte finish on a panel; it also includes a paperlike feel and low-power, monochrome modes that create a reasonable facsimile of an E Ink screen. But the matte effect has always been the biggest draw for me. … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
I’ve spent most of the last couple weeks using an otherwise unexceptional midrange Android phone with one amazing feature: a matte OLED display. That screen is by far the best thing about the TCL P80 Ultra, and weirdly, it’s made me more excited for the iPhone Duo and its matte inner display.

2023’s TCL Nxtpaper 40 first brought matte displays to the company’s phones after they appeared on tablets in 2021. Nxtpaper is more than a simple matte finish on a panel; it also includes a paperlike feel and low-power, monochrome modes that create a reasonable facsimile of an E Ink screen. But the matte effect has always been the biggest draw for me.

The P80 Ultra’s screen is special because it’s the first to combine the Nxtpaper tech with an OLED panel. That means it’s the best-looking Nxtpaper screen yet, with deeper blacks, better contrast, and richer colors. Previous models have felt a little visually compromised; this one doesn’t. It also finally enables an always-on display. Always-on displays have been the norm on Android for years, and the fact that TCL’s Nxtpaper phones didn’t have them was a dealbreaker for many.

The P80 Ultra has a triple rear camera, but it’s nothing special.

The Nxtpaper Key on the side triggers e-reader-inspired screen modes.

The OLED screen looks great for photos and videos.

And the viewing angles are unmatched.

I’ve used a couple of Nxtpaper phones over the last few years, but usually found the tradeoffs — both across the specs and in the screen itself — never quite made sense. In some respects, that’s still true for the P80 Ultra, which I can’t entirely recommend as a phone in its own right. Performance has been sluggish and stuttering, and while the triple rear camera has decent enough specs on paper, photo quality is distinctly average.

The difference now is that the display feels like all upside. As an OLED, it’s bright and beautiful, with enough color and contrast to suit both scrolling and streaming. But the matte finish keeps it comfortable to look at, even at cranked-up brightness or in a dimly lit room, with less flicker and blue light than most other displays. Nxtpaper’s anti-glare effect actually makes this a really excellent phone to use in brighter environments. It looked great under the bright lights of TCL’s IFA trade show booth, no mean feat. And the viewing angles are truly excellent, with good visibility even when the phone is almost entirely side-on. That’s without touching on the texture, which is smooth and satiny, so your finger sticks just a little less when swiping. It’s a small thing, but a welcome one.

Because this is a Nxtpaper phone, it goes a little further. A dedicated toggle on the phone’s side triggers one of two more substantial overhauls to the display. Paper Mode washes out the display’s color — or can go fully monochromatic if you prefer — to make it even easier on your eyes, with the option to exclude individual apps so they run as usual. Streaming apps and games are exempted by default. Max Ink Mode is more drastic: It’s strictly monochrome and removes access to most apps and OS features, giving you a power-efficient mode with minimal distractions, turning the P80 Ultra into something between an e-reader and a dumb phone.

Although most other phones are limited to aftermarket matte screen protectors to get anything like the same effect, TCL isn’t the only manufacturer making hardware with a matte display. Huawei has made a string of tablets with what it calls PaperMatte panels, and Lenovo and Xiaomi offer similar screens on select models. Matte screens underpin the painterly effect of Samsung’s Frame TVs (and imitations from rivals including TCL). And then, of course, there’s Apple’s nano-texture glass.

Apple’s offered this coating as an option on iPad Pro models since 2024, selling it on the basis that its paperlike qualities are beneficial to anyone using the iPad Pro as a drawing device. It’s now appearing on a phone for the first time with the iPhone Duo, with Apple relying on the anti-glare effect to minimize the visibility of the foldable panel’s crease.

I haven’t had the chance to try the Duo yet, but using the P80 Ultra has made me more excited to. Pairing a matte effect with the Duo’s large inner screen sounds great, and it’s one of the few elements of the Duo that no Android foldable can currently match. My only hesitation is that Apple didn’t make the outer panel matte too — an odd choice given how much it’s emphasized the seamless switch between the two screens — so I worry the transition might be jarring. Given the book-style form factor, Apple will also be missing a trick if it doesn’t create its own e-reader-inspired mode for the Duo to match TCL’s, though the existing grayscale mode might be a decent imitation.

Perhaps what’s most exciting about an iPhone adopting a matte panel is that within the year we’ll probably see Android brands imitate it, something TCL wasn’t able to inspire. We’ve already seen the Duo’s squat form factor appear in handsets from Samsung, Xiaomi, and Huawei, with Motorola teasing its own too. The Duo’s matte layer hasn’t yet sparked its own imitators, but I suspect it’s only a matter of time, especially if it helps hide foldable creases. Not every phone needs to be matte, but I would love more of them to give me the option. Hopefully Apple’s industry influence grants me my wish.

title: Samsung Galaxy Tab S12 series goes official from $1,199 with Photoshop pre-installed
snippet: Samsung is today officially launching its new Galaxy Tab S12 series with the Tab S12+ and Tab S12 Ultra delivering big displays, powerful specs, and some new software tricks too. more…
fullText:
Samsung is today officially launching its new Galaxy Tab S12 series with the Tab S12+ and Tab S12 Ultra delivering big displays, powerful specs, and some new software tricks too.

Available starting October 7, the Galaxy Tab S12+ and Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra continue Samsung’s flagship tablet series with some nominal upgrades. While they’re visually almost identical to prior generations, there are some spec bumps, including the new MediaTek Dimensity 9500.

Galaxy Tab S12+

12.6-inch 120Hz AMOLED display (2800×1752), in-display fingerprint sensor

MediaTek Dimensity 9500

187.8 x 289.5 x 5.3 mm

Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra

Besides the size, one of the notable differences is that there’s no cellular version of the Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra. Samsung has no smaller screen size available this year, with the Galaxy Tab S11 still serving as the 11-inch option.

Both tablets, Samsung says, include a larger vapor chamber for heat dissipation, retain the IP68 dust/water resistance rating of prior models, and ship with One UI 9 (Android 17) out of the box with seven years of OS + security updates. There’s also an S Pen included in the box, with a keyboard cover and other accessories available as add-on purchases.

	

Samsung has new partnerships with productivity apps, too. Adobe Photoshop is pre-installed on the Galaxy Tab S12 series. The app has S Pen optimization and users get four months of free access to the app as well. Notability, a recent arrival on Android, is also pre-loaded and comes with a six-month trial. There are further freebies in Goodnotes, LumaFusion, Notion, and others, as well as a six-month Google AI Pro trial for boosted Gemini capabilities.

Galaxy Tab S12+ starts at $1,199, while Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra starts at $1,399, the latter being a $100 increase over last year. As mentioned, both are available in the US starting October 7.

fullText:
Sporting a 100% Rotten Tomatoes score, the extreme mountain climbing documentary “The Last First: Winter K2” is now available to Apple TV subscribers. Watch the trailer below.

’A complex, harrowing and moving story’

A few weeks ago, Apple TV released the trailer for “The Last First: Winter K2” and celebrated reaching a 100% score on Rotten Tomatoes’ Tomatometer.

The documentary, which has also premiered in selected theaters in recent days, promises “an unflinching look at the industry of extreme mountain climbing and its changing culture.”

“The Last First: Winter K2” is directed by Amir Bar-Lev (The Tillman Story, Long Strange Trip – The Untold Story of The Grateful Dead) and focuses on a 2021 expedition to the summit of Mount Godwin-Austen, better known as K2.

Here’s Apple TV on what subscribers can expect from “The Last First: Winter K2”:

Focusing on a 2021 expedition, this documentary follows Icelander John Snorri Sigurjónsson and the Pakistani father-son team of Ali and Sajid Sadpara, a party of mountaineers who set out to be the first to summit K2 in the winter, when the mountain’s conditions are the cruelest. The men soon find themselves sharing the treacherous ascent with influencer climbers and their film crews, commercial expedition clients and a Nepalese team no longer content to help Westerners achieve mountaineering glory. “The Last First: Winter K2” takes us to the icy heights and unpredictable weather of K2 and reveals a surprising and layered story — one of strategy and determination, class and caste, money and power — all under life-and-death circumstances.

title: iOS 27 adds four new ways to customize your iPhone’s Lock Screen
snippet: iOS 27 continues Apple’s trend of giving you more control over the design of your iPhone’s Lock Screen. This year, there are new customization options, wallpaper settings, and more. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 continues Apple’s trend of giving you more control over the design of your iPhone’s Lock Screen. This year, there are new customization options, wallpaper settings, and more.

Extend wallpapers

iOS 27 brings new Apple Intelligence editing features to the Photos app. This includes a revamped version of Clean Up, as well as a Reframe. Another new option is Extend, which intelligently expands your image so you can adjust its aspect ratio, straighten horizons, or just add more space around the edges.

As seen above, the Extend feature also comes to the Lock Screen in iOS 27. If a photo doesn’t match your iPhone’s aspect ratio or isn’t cropped quite right for a wallpaper, iOS 27 will automatically suggest using Extend to fix it.

Extend will use AI to generate additional image content around the edges, so you have more flexibility when setting a picture as your iPhone’s wallpaper.

Generate your own wallpapers

iOS 27 brings big improvements to Image Playground, which is Apple’s app that lets you generate images using artificial intelligence. The changes to Image Playground also come to your iPhone’s Lock Screen. Now, you can generate wallpapers using Image Playground right from the wallpaper picker in Settings or on the Lock Screen itself.

In the wallpaper picker, you’ll see a new “Image Playground” option. The feature will create stylized versions of images from your Photos library, such as “Retro Illustration” and “Animation.”

You can also create a custom wallpaper from scratch just by describing what you want in natural language.

Move the clock

iOS 27 finally lets you shrink the clock on your iPhone’s Lock Screen. While Apple has let you customize the clock’s size for several years, iOS 27 goes a step further. Now, you can move the clock on your Lock Screen up to the top row of widgets.

This frees up space on your Lock Screen so you can see more of your wallpaper. It does, of course, come at the expense of being able to glance at the time from far away. For many people, though, the point of the Lock Screen is to show off wallpapers, and iOS 27 makes that even easier.

With iOS 27, you can now swipe away the Now Playing widget that appears on your iPhone’s Lock Screen. Even if you clear the Now Playing widget, whatever you’re listening to will continue playing.

This is great if you find yourself accidentally tapping the Now Playing widget on your Lock Screen.

Wrap up

What do you think of the new Lock Screen customization features in iOS 27? Let us know down in the comments.

snippet: Apple TV currently has a packed lineup of new shows airing, and it’s about to add another. Small Prophets is a British comedy premiering next week that has a 100% Rotten Tomatoes score. Here’s the trailer. more…
fullText:
Apple TV currently has a packed lineup of new shows airing, and it’s about to add another. Small Prophets is a British comedy premiering next week that has a 100% Rotten Tomatoes score. Here’s the trailer.

Small Prophets debuts October 7 on Apple TV, and it’s already beloved by viewers and critics

Last month, Apple TV announced that it was doing something very rare: licensing an existing show from another network.

British comedy Small Prophets debuted in the UK earlier this year and became a hit for the BBC—it has a 100% Rotten Tomatoes score. Now Apple will bring the beloved show to viewers around the world.

Small Prophets premieres Wednesday, October 7 on Apple TV with its first two episodes, followed by weekly releases through November 4.

Today Apple debuted the trailer for Small Prophets, offering a taste of what’s coming. Here’s the series summary, followed by the trailer:

“Small Prophets” is a comic tale of the eccentric Michael Sleep (Quigley) who, since his darling Clea disappeared seven years ago, has lived a very ordinary life. He works in a DIY store, visits his dad Brian (Palin) and hopes for Clea to return. One day Brian shares an old recipe involving rainwater, horse manure and more than a little alchemy. With recipe in hand, Michael sets out (albeit with some skepticism) to create homunculi — magical spirits that can predict the future — in the hope they have the answer to his burning question: “will I ever see Clea again?”

Small Prophets was created, written, and directed by Mackenzie Crook, who also created Detectorists and acted in The Office (UK) and Pirates of the Caribbean.

Note: Small Prophets will be available globally on Apple TV, but UK viewers won’t gain access until 2027.

Currently airing Apple TV comedies include Brothers with Matthew McConaughey and Ted Lasso season 4. Owen Wilson’s hit series Stick returns soon too.

Apple TV is available for $14.99 per month, or you can get it discounted through the Apple One bundle.

title: Google Pixel at 10: Successes, failures, and fun along the way [Video]
snippet: A decade of Pixel, it’s only in the last few years that we have seen Google settle into a rhythm with smartphones. It hasn’t been smooth sailing, though. more…
fullText:
A decade of Pixel, it’s only in the last few years that we have seen Google settle into a rhythm with smartphones. It hasn’t been smooth sailing, though.

Look back at the line-up, and it’s still hard to believe we’ve had a decade of Pixel. If you asked me back in 2016 whether Google’s in-house hardware experiment would stick around long enough to reach fully custom 3nm silicon, I’m not sure I’d have believed you.

To say that Google was late to the market is an understatement. By 2016, Apple and Samsung were already well into the swing of things. To be fair, that still is the case a decade later, but now with an even tighter iron grip over the space. I was personally distraught when the Nexus lineup was canceled to the point that I actually went with the Galaxy S8 rather than wait to see what Google had in store next.

	

Google’s answer to the ‘big two’ was Pixel. A phone not “officially” made by partners, but still sort of relying on OEMs while the production pipeline or groundwork was laid.

Pixel and Pixel XL (2016)

The original Google Pixel was built in a close manufacturing partnership with HTC, featuring a wedge-shaped profile that famously tapered down to eliminate any camera bump. 

Let’s be real, the hardware wasn’t tearing up trees, and it looked more than a little similar to the iPhone 7/8 series. It was a conservative design, but pretty darn self-assured.

The main thing that helped differentiate the device was its built-in Google Assistant integration and HDR+ image processing pipeline for photos. Rightly or wrongly, this simple formula has more or less defined the Pixel for the past decade of Google’s mobile computing efforts.

Smart, simple software and artificial intelligence have been at the forefront from the very beginning and will remain so over the next 10 years.

Pixel 2 series (2017)

With the second generation, Google finally figured out design. The LG-made Pixel 2 XL gave us the iconic “Panda” colorway with its stark black-and-white glass back and the bright orange accent power button. You’ve told us time and time again that it’s a personal favorite for Pixel fans. It also debuted the Pixel Visual Core, Google’s first attempt at custom co-processing to let apps like Instagram use HDR+.

Add single-lens Portrait Mode that put dual-camera rivals to shame, squeeze-to-activate Active Edge, ambient Now Playing track identification, and the persistent At a Glance widget, and the Pixel 2 series genuinely felt like magic in your hand.

The first major problems started to appear, though. The blue shift on the 2 XL meant that viewing from an angle is not recommended. Screen burn-in was also something people suffered.

Pixel 3 series (2018)

The Pixel 3 era was peak camera software dominance mixed with a few just flat-out bizarre hardware choices. 

That Pixel 3 XL “bathtub” notch was an absolute eyesore and was thoroughly roasted by the tech community and reviewers alike. I think in some ways, once you fired up the camera, all was forgiven. I’ve taken some incredible photos with the Pixel 3. Pictures that I still look at very fondly 8 years later.

This was the first Pixel to come with Night Sight, which arrived via a software update and single-handedly changed low-light smartphone photography forever. It wasn’t the first, but it was one of the best implementations.

You could shoot in near pitch-black conditions and walk away with a clean, detailed photo without ever touching the flash. Pair that with yet more AI-powered functions such as Call Screen, which handles telemarketers and spam in real time, and the software was doing all the heavy lifting.

In trademark fashion, the Pixel 3 had issues with RAM management and poor battery life. It was a mixed bag, but it was followed up by something truly interesting because the Pixel 3a is one of the best midrangers ever. It set the stage for a change of pace…but that wasn’t for a couple of years.

Pixel 4 series (2019)

Let’s be honest, Google swung for the fences with the Pixel 4, but it didn’t quite land. 

It is almost the least Pixel-y of the entire lineup because it stands apart from all that have since followed. The black sheep in many ways. It ditched the trusty rear fingerprint scanner, they threw Project Soli into a chunky top bezel for wave-to-snooze Motion Sense gestures and 3D Face Unlock.

We also got a silky smooth 90Hz display and a telephoto lens rather than the industry-preferred and marginally more flexible ultrawide. It felt like a zig to everyone else’s zag.

Alas, it was a big risk and one that ended up compromising the most. The small Pixel 4 had a tiny 2,800 mAh battery that struggled to get through an afternoon, let alone a full day. High launch prices and Soli radar frequency restrictions in key markets meant commercial success was hard to come by, and the negatives really held back the lineup. It actually triggered a reshuffle in Google’s hardware team.

Pixel 4a, 4a 5G and Pixel 5 (2020)

Faced with global disruptions in 2020 due to the emergence of COVID-19 and maybe due to some, at the time, unknown future plans, Google completely pivoted with the Pixel lineup. The Pixel 4 was a big swing, but the follow-up series went in a very different direction.

The mid-range Pixel 4a launched at just $349/£349 and became an immediate hit because it kept that flagship-grade camera performance in an understated, no-nonsense plastic body. This was an appetizer for what was to come.

Then came the flagship Pixel 5, but this wasn’t the premium phone that many expected. It skipped top-tier Qualcomm silicon entirely for the upper-mid-range Snapdragon 765G. It was the same chip used by many cheaper phones and even the more affordable Pixel 4a 5G, which was basically a bigger, bolder version of the 4a.

The 5 was coated in a bio-resin finish over a recycled aluminum frame, it brought back the rear fingerprint scanner, swapped the telephoto for an ultrawide lens, and gave us uniform bezels with reliable battery life. It lacked raw processing grunt, but it earned a cult following for simply being a reliable, compact everyday phone.

On one hand, it was good to see Google right some issues with the previous generation. On the other hand, it was confusing as it sort of signaled that maybe Pixels were not high-end phones. It was a reset.

Pixel 6 series (2021)

After a fairly unassuming and, arguably, boring preamble, 2021 was without a doubt the biggest turning point in Pixel history. 

Google overhauled the design, introducing the now iconic camera bar running across the back, creating a silhouette you could spot from a mile away. We were given a proper two-tier lineup with a Pro phone that packed in a triple camera system, a larger 120Hz display, and a cheaper but still competent base model. 

Most importantly, though, was the debut of original Tensor (now G1) silicon. Moving away from standard Qualcomm chips meant Google could tailor hardware directly for on-device ML—powering features like Magic Eraser, Live Translate, and Material You dynamic color themes.

As well-received as it was at launch, the Pixel 6 had some serious growing pains with a slow optical fingerprint reader, terrible modem performance, and overheating issues galore, but despite what were fairly major issues, the foundation was set.

Pixel 7 series (2022)

The Pixel 7 and 7 Pro took the foundational groundwork of the Pixel 6 and smoothed out the rough edges. Visually, the camera bar evolved into a seamless piece of 100% recycled aluminum that flowed directly out of the side rails, swapping out the all-glass visor for a sleeker metal shell with pill-and-cutout camera cutouts.

Under the hood sat Tensor G2, which paired with an upgraded Samsung Exynos 5300 modem. This finally resolved the signal drops and battery drain that plagued the previous generation. While raw computational gains were modest, Tensor G2 unlocked key software capabilities: Photo Unblur in Google Photos (which could restore old, blurry archival photos taken on any camera), Macro Focus via the ultrawide lens, and the return of a fast 2D Face Unlock system.

Mid-2023 also saw the Pixel lineup expand its footprint. The Pixel 7a raised the bar for mid-range phones by bringing a 90Hz refresh rate and wireless charging to the A-series for the first time. Meanwhile, Google made its long-awaited entry into new form factors with the original Pixel Fold, showcasing a short, wide “passport” design that prioritized a usable outer display over tall, narrow screens. It was a bit of a “fail” in the sense that it didn’t move the needle and was quickly overshadowed by others due to launching with the previous-generation processor and, admittedly, strange aspect ratios.

Pixel 8 series (2023)

In my mind, the Pixel 8 and 8 Pro were the moment the lineup transitioned from an enthusiast recommendation with caveats to a phone you could comfortably recommend to everyday consumers. Never perfect, but quietly the last Pixel that felt truly like a Pixel. These are bubbly, friendly phones in all the ways that matter.

A few more AI functions made their debut: Best Take, Audio Magic Eraser, Video Boost, and, as a headline addition, 7 years of full updates for the first time. Basically, making these the industry standard for smartphone support. Google leapfrogged Samsung and even Apple for software support windows.

No, no reinvention of the wheel. Tensor still didn’t hit the heights many wanted, which is to say it was fine.

Pixel 9 series (2024)

The Pixel 9 was a rapid design departure in a number of ways. Firstly, it ditched the friendly, playful looks that had been a trademark of the series. Instead, it took a very boxy route that instantly felt familiar to anyone who may have tried an iPhone.

It was a really polished upgrade and sort of put to bed some of the tricky hardware issues that plagued many of the older Pixel models. Google also began leaning into yet more AI-powered functionality, with Gemini now being a key component.

Google unified the launch across all phones, coming on day one, but also switched from the standard October release cadence to a late-summer August release. Pitching the Pixel ahead of the iPhone has been a huge change. Allowing the company to lay out plans and getting even more hype around a launch lineup.

Pixel 10 series (2025)

Although on the surface, almost the exact same, the Pixel 10 was the first 3nm chip for the lineup, and it was the first to be fabricated by TSMC. It signaled the end of the Samsung Foundry partnership that was the start of the Tensor era.

Any lingering thermal issues were gone, Gemini was integrated even further and into even more places, like the camera, and the first steps of multimodel intelligence were added with Magic Cue. I’d stop short of saying the Pixel 10 delivers on some of the promises made way back on October 4, 2016, but it came as close as it ever had until that point.

Finally, we had a flagship-level device with Qi2 magnets at the back too. It took until 2025 for one of the biggest Android brands to adopt Magsafe or, in this case, Pixelsnap. With that one move, the Pixel 10 opened up a whole world of accessories to be attached without the need for a case. It’s so elementary, it’s a wonder we haven’t seen more try to do it.

Pixel 11 series (2026) and beyond

A decade later, we’re here with the Pixel 11. The peak of the Made by Google series thus far. There are still pain points, namely a design that hasn’t evolved too drastically, performance from the Tensor processor still feels decidedly mid-range at times, and a heavy emphasis on AI functionality to make up for this raw performance gap.

A sometimes lazy observation of the original Pixel was that it was the “iPhone of Android,” but that seems to have been taken to heart, and a decade after launch, we have the most “iPhone-y” Pixel to date. Maybe that is a symptom of where smartphones have stalled, but it’s a really interesting evolution. The advantage is that you know what to expect. Gemini is becoming more and more prominent and yet a more integral component in Pixel phones, and that isn’t likely to cease any time soon.

What’s easy to see is that Pixel has been a bigger success than the Nexus lineup. Getting hold of the full end-to-end user experience has helped drastically. I don’t think anyone can argue that the best Nexus phone is easily surpassed by the best Pixel phone.

It would be remiss of anyone talking about Google products without some fears over whether we’ll get another decade of Pixel, but with so many internal changes at the company and bigger marketing budgets thrown at actually marketing the devices, it seems that, at least for now, the Pixel is here to stay. 

The past decade has proved that Google was never really trying to build the highest-spec hardware on the market. Instead, Pixel has always been an engine designed to deliver Google’s software vision. From early HDR+ algorithms on single camera lens setups and now to custom TSMC Tensor silicon wired for Gemini integration, it’s hard to argue that Google’s Pixel has succeeded in changing how we evaluate a smartphone: not by how fast its CPU clocks, but by how helpful it is throughout the day.

Maybe sales will eventually catch up, but the main thing is to keep making solid devices, and playing the long game might start to be the best decision Google could have made after entering the market late.

There have been plenty of bumps in the road along the way, but here’s the next decade of Pixel. I’m sure it’ll be a wild ride.

title: These are the best times to save money on your next flight, according to Google Flights
snippet: Ahead of the busy holiday travel season, Google is detailing the best time to book your next flight to get the best possible price. more…
fullText:
Ahead of the busy holiday travel season, Google is detailing the best time to book your next flight to get the best possible price.

With surging fuel prices have also come much higher plane ticket costs and, with that, everyone’s looking for a deal. In a blog post this week, Google Flights details the best times to book your next flight.

For domestic US flights, the best time is apparently 39 days prior to departure, but the lowest price can fall anywhere between 57 days prior and 22 days prior to the actual flight date. International flights should be booked much further out, with 89 days being the magic number there.

Thanksgiving and Christmas flights bend the rules a bit. Thanksgiving flights are actually cheapest 34 days prior to departure, but Christmas flights need to be booked much earlier at around 56 days.

	

Here’s the full breakdown from Google:

Domestic flights: 39 days before departure (low price range is 22–57 days)

International flights: 89 days before departure, but the average price drop during the low range (50–133 days out) is insignificant

Thanksgiving: Lowest prices hit 34 days before departure (low price range is 21–57 days)

Christmas: 56 days before departure (low price range is 33–67 days)

Spring break: 50 days before departure (low price range is 29–64 days) for trips in March or April

Summer vacation: 21 days before departure (low price range is 20–47 days) for trips in July or August

Trips to Europe: 49 days or more before departure

Trips to Mexico or the Caribbean: 43 days before departure (low price range is 24–69 days)

The post goes on to detail trending destinations for the 2026 travel season, with Hawaii being the top Thanksgiving destination and international trips to Greece and Canada trending around Christmas and New Year’s Eve.

title: Google confirms Android Auto updates & fixes for media apps – the squiggly line is here to stay
snippet: New Android Auto updates tend to be a bit strange, with changes often showing up for some users but not others, but Google has just recapped a handful of Android Auto updates for media apps from the past few months, including confirmation that the squiggly line design is here to stay. more…
fullText:
New Android Auto updates tend to be a bit strange, with changes often showing up for some users but not others, but Google has just recapped a handful of Android Auto updates for media apps from the past few months, including confirmation that the squiggly line design is here to stay.

In a Reddit post by Google’s “Community Engagement Manager” for Android, five recent Android Auto updates are confirmed as either rolling out or widely available. The first is the ability to control media from any app, including YouTube and others. We noticed this rolling out back in March of this year for YouTube, and it has since rolled out to more apps. Today’s post confirms it is available for “browser audio streams, and niche media apps” and is designed to work with “any media app.” You can use it for play/pause and skip controls, but you can’t open an app to browse any other data.

Next up is the redesigned media app player that applies to apps like Spotify, YouTube Music, and Pocket Casts. The new design makes it easier to access playback controls and also better fits on a variety of different screen sizes.

This one has been showing up all year and started rolling out more broadly in July. Today’s post confirms that the in-app UI for media apps on Android Auto will start changing for some apps “in the next few months,” as announced in May.

	

Another new media-focused feature on Android Auto that’s been rolling out is the ability to swipe between active media sessions from the dashboard widget. If you start driving with one app and then switch to another, both will stay readily available for easy access.

A background improvement, Google’s post adds, has been made to autoplay. This includes making it so media apps that you haven’t recently used will “no longer be selected for autoplay,” while Android Auto will also now recognize if you frequently stop autoplay and offer a pop-up that lets you turn off the feature quickly. If you’ve ever noticed issues with autoplay starting even when you have it turned off right after your vehicle turns out, Google also says that a fix is being applied.

Finally, the post also confirms that the “squiggly line” media player design is here to stay. This one has been showing up for months, but has come and gone for many. Especially in the past few weeks, there have been dozens of reports of the redesign simply vanishing.

The updated design is apparently meant to “make it easier to see where you are in a track at a glance,” but Google is apparently listening for feedback on it – it’s been a rather divisive change among the Android Auto community.

title: Gemini app gains new ‘Map’ tool, replacing ‘/’ with ‘@’
snippet: Google has introduced a “Map” tool to aid your location-based Gemini app prompts on Android and iOS. Meanwhile, the Gemini app is already getting ready to replace the forward slash for skills. more…
fullText:
Google has introduced a “Map” tool to aid your location-based Gemini app prompts on Android and iOS. Meanwhile, the Gemini app is already getting ready to replace the forward slash for skills.

On mobile (not available on the web), you can find “Map” at the end of the carousel alongside Photos, Camera, Avatar, Files, Drive, and Notebooks. 

This launches a live map of your current location with a circular focus area. You can pan and zoom in/out as needed, while the magnifying glass icon in the top-right corner lets you search for any location. Once you’ve made a selection, hit “Explore this area.”

This adds “Map Area” to the prompt box where you can append text. The Map tool is widely rolled out.

	

With the latest Google app beta (version 17.63), Gemini is replacing the forward slash (“/”) to invoke skills with the “@” symbol that’s already used for Connected Apps, which will soon be renamed to “Connectors.”

Google just announced on Wednesday that skills will replace Gems and that you can use a slash in the prompt box to activate. We’re seeing the following prompt when entering a slash: 

/ is now @. Access your skills, connectors and more from a single place.

The box that appears is slightly wider than before, with skills appearing first and a shortcut to create new ones. This change is not widely rolled out yet.

Gemini app adding Google Wallet integration for ‘personalized insights’

title: Amazon responds to data center backlash, says it no longer uses NDAs
snippet: The CEO of Amazon Web Services tried to push back against widespread suspicion of data centers.
fullText:
Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman said the company has stopped using nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) in its dealings with government agencies as it seeks approval to build new data centers.

Garman’s statement is just one sentence in a longer blog post in which he tried to push back against widespread suspicion of data centers, and to make the case that they’re actually good for communities.

NDAs are a significant piece of the broader data center backlash. For example, environmental activist Erin Brockovich recently said that the number one complaint she’s heard about data centers is transparency, with these projects following a common pattern: “projects announced after permits are already secured, developers who don’t return calls, local officials who signed NDAs before their neighbors knew a project was being considered.”

As a result of that backlash, New York announced a one-year moratorium on permits for large data centers, and, according to Garman, there are more than 100 data center moratoriums currently being considered across the United States.

“If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations,” Garman claimed. “As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position.”

Garman also attempted to puncture what he said are four big myths around data centers: that they consume too much water, that they increase electricity costs, that they emit an enormous amount of pollution, and that they don’t provide any benefits to their communities.

Pointing to an Amazon report about its own water usage, Garman said that “direct data center water consumption” only accounts for 0.5% of all industrial water usage in the United States, “orders of magnitude less than golf courses, almond farming, and many other industries.”

Nvidia recently said its new cooling system eliminates “pretty much all water usage” inside the data center, but those claims — like Amazon’s — seem to ignore the broader water usage involved in electricity generation and chip manufacturing. Scientists have also said they need to study data centers’ water and energy usage independently, since there are no federal or state requirements around how tech companies report this data. 

As for electricity rates, Garman said they’ve only gone up in some states with large numbers of data centers, while they’ve gone down or at least grown more slowly in others. And he argued, “In instances where energy rates are going up, it’s primarily because the grid is old and hasn’t been invested in and expanded before the demand arrived.”

On the other hand, an independent watchdog said recently data centers were the main culprit behind a 76% year-over-year price increase on America’s largest electrical grid.

When it comes to pollution — an issue that the NAACP is currently suing Elon Musk’s SpaceX/xAI over — Garman complained that critics focus on the maximum amount of pollution allowed under data center permits. For example, a planned Amazon data center in Texas is permitted to release 33 million tons of carbon dioxide per year, which is more than any other power plant in the United States.

“The truth is data center generators almost never run,” Garman said. “They’re idle 99.9% of the time (they run roughly 10 hours per year, mostly for required maintenance testing).”

As for the community benefits, this is where Garman wrote, “We no longer use nondisclosure agreements with the government agencies we work with on our projects.” Plus, he said, “Over the past three years, Amazon has contributed more than $1 billion to communities across the U.S. in which we have a meaningful data center presence.”

Will this be enough to quell community suspicion? Perhaps not — Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei recently argued that the AI backlash is “fundamentally a crisis of trust,” where people assume governments and tech companies are always “cooking up some new way to screw them over.” Similarly, writer Jasmine Sun noted that when data center opponents are presented with the tech companies’ arguments, their response is usually, “I don’t believe them.”

Anthony Ha is TechCrunch’s weekend editor. Previously, he worked as a tech reporter at Adweek, a senior editor at VentureBeat, a local government reporter at the Hollister Free Lance, and vice president of content at a VC firm. He lives in New York City.

Still carrying the full MSRP over at Amazon, it is very hard to believe this model drops this low in new condition for fall Prime Day. We did see it drop to $399 in mid-September, but it has otherwise remained at full price.

title: Apple faces renewed scrutiny over removal of ICEBlock from the App Store
snippet: CNN reports that Rep. Jamie Raskin sent a letter to Apple this week challenging the company’s explanation for removing ICEBlock from the App Store last year. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
CNN reports that Rep. Jamie Raskin sent a letter to Apple this week challenging the company’s explanation for removing ICEBlock from the App Store last year. Here are the details.

ICEBlock removal once again under scrutiny

According to CNN, Apple sent a letter to Rep. Jamie Raskin last July explaining its decision to remove ICEBlock and similar apps from the App Store, and Raskin has now responded with new questions about the company’s justification.

For context, ICEBlock was one of the most prominent apps that allowed users to report and track ICE activity in their area. The app rapidly rose in popularity during the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, growing from around 20,000 users to roughly one million within weeks.

As its popularity skyrocketed, ICEBlock became the target of the US government, with then-Attorney General Pam Bondi publicly calling for Apple to remove the app and warning its developer that he could face prosecution.

Following pressure from the DOJ, Apple removed it and several similar apps from the App Store, citing concerns over the safety of federal agents. The move came shortly after a gunman opened fire on an ICE facility in Dallas, ultimately killing two detainees in an attack that federal authorities described as targeted violence against ICE.

This, in turn, prompted Raskin to investigate whether the Trump administration had pressured Apple and Google into removing ICE-tracking apps, and what impact those removals may have had on constitutionally protected speech.

As part of that investigation, CNN reports that Apple sent Raskin a letter last July explaining why it removed ICEBlock and similar apps from the App Store.

From CNN:

Apple says its decision to remove ICEBlock and similar platforms from the app store last year was prompted by concerns — including those raised by the Trump administration — about agent safety following a fatal shooting that left two detainees dead at a Dallas Immigration and Customs Enforcement office.

Apple’s explanation came in a July letter to Rep. Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat and ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, who earlier this year launched an investigation into the Justice Department’s role in the removal of the apps from Apple’s and Google’s app stores and the impact on constitutionally protected speech. The letter has not previously been reported.

CNN says that Apple’s letter to Raskin also mentioned that the company approved ICEBlock in April 2025, after developer Joshua Aaron addressed what Apple referred to as “certain user privacy concerns.”

Apple also reportedly said it continued to monitor news coverage and criticism of the app in the months that followed, ultimately deciding to remove ICEBlock and similar apps after concluding they violated its App Store guidelines by providing “precise location information about ICE officers,” which could potentially be used for targeted attacks.

Apple also cited concerns raised by Bondi after the Dallas shooting, as well as comments from FBI Director Kash Patel that the shooter had searched for apps that tracked ICE agents’ locations.

According to Apple, those concerns, together with what it described as a broader increase in ICE activity and threats against agents, prompted the company to conduct a new review of ICEBlock.

Raskin pushes back

According to CNN, Raskin sent a letter to Apple this week further questioning the company’s justification for removing ICEBlock and similar apps from the App Store.

	

From CNN:

Raskin said the move suggests that Apple may be “working with the government to violate its customers’ First Amendment rights to record and report on the activities of their own government” in a response letter sent Monday to Apple’s senior director of government affairs, Timothy Powderly.

CNN also notes that Raskin disputed Apple’s reliance on the Dallas shooting, arguing that the gunman did not need an ICE-tracking app to locate a fixed government facility and reportedly found the address using “an app that comes standard on Apple devices.”

He also pointed to other navigation apps that remain available on the App Store despite providing real-time information about law enforcement locations, and asked Apple to conduct a new independent review of the removals and provide a full list of apps it removed in response to concerns raised by the DOJ.

Apple Upgrade lowers the entry cost of iPhone Duo substantially, here are the details

Apple Upgrade launched recently as a way to lease Apple products at low monthly prices. I was initially skeptical, but it’s a surprisingly good deal for one reason: you always have the option of buying your device when the lease ends, and your total cost will never exceed the original list price.

If you perpetually keep leasing products, you’ll pay more in the long run. But if you use Apple Upgrade to get products with a low upfront cost, and pay them off later, it can be a great option. And that’s very evident with iPhone Duo pricing.

Apple’s website has a variety of options for getting an iPhone Duo. You can buy outright for $1,999 for the 256GB model, or do 24-month financing for $83/month.

But with Apple Upgrade, a 24-month lease is $57.99/month. And if you trade in a recent iPhone, you can even get an iPhone Duo for as low as $9/month.

iPhone Duo 12-month lease: $9.24/month with trade-in of iPhone 17 Pro Max

iPhone Duo 24-month lease: $21.12/month with trade-in of iPhone 17 Pro Max

	

Trading in a product like iPhone 17 Pro Max takes a significant amount off the monthly cost. And if you decide to buy the iPhone Duo outright at the end of your lease term, that trade-in credit is still fully applied.

However, if you decide to trade in the iPhone Duo in a year or two to get a new model (like the rumored iPhone 20 Pro), just know that your monthly cost will go up a lot, since you’ll no longer have the discount of a device trade-in.

All this to say, if the sticker shock of $2,000 made the Duo seem unattainable, it may not be.

title: Report: Meta’s Muse crosses 5 million downloads amid massive advertising push
snippet: Meta’s streak at the top of the App Store continues in the US and Canada, as its AI assistant Muse is now past 5 million downloads, according to Sensor Tower. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Meta’s streak at the top of the App Store continues in the US and Canada, as its AI assistant Muse is now past 5 million downloads, according to Sensor Tower. Here are the details.

Muse continues its 12-day streak at the top of the US App Store

Three weeks ago, Meta launched Muse in the US. Soon after, it overtook ChatGPT as the top free app in the US App Store

Today, according to a projection by Sensor Tower Senior Insights Analyst Kara Lee, Muse crossed 5 million downloads. That means it reached the milestone considerably faster than ChatGPT, Grok, and Claude, which the market intelligence firm says took 56, 103, and 492 days, respectively.

Source: Sensor Tower

Muse is Meta’s agentic AI assistant, capable of browsing the web and carrying out tasks on a user’s behalf, including sending emails, shopping, filling out forms, and booking travel.

Sensor Tower adds that Claude and Grok were iOS-exclusive in their first 5 days. Meta’s Muse app, by contrast, is available on iOS and Android, but only in the US and Canada.

Here’s Sensor Tower with more context on how Muse’s 5 million-download milestone compares to other major app launches:

According to Sensor Tower estimates, only 23 apps have reached over 5mn US downloads within 22 days of launch. ~85% of these apps are mobile gaming apps, including Fortnite, Pokemon GO, Candy Crush, and more. There were only 3 apps within that list that are not gaming apps, including Disney+, HBO Max, and Threads, which received ~20mn, 18mn, and 14mn downloads during that time, respectively.

According to Sensor Tower data, Muse has received the largest share of Meta’s house ads, accounting for up to 50% of daily house impressions over the past two weeks (9/14-927), as Facebook and WhatsApp ceded share of impressions during the same period.

Sensor Tower also says Muse ranked among the top 15 brands by advertising impressions in the US during the week of September 21 through September 27.

title: Galaxy S27 Ultra’s missing camera shown in leaks is its 3x zoom
snippet: Previous Galaxy S27 Ultra leaks have directed attention to the new camera island, but don’t overlook the missing camera lens left behind with the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Apparently, that camera is the Samsung Galaxy S27 Ultra’s 10MP 3x zoom. more…
fullText:
Previous Galaxy S27 Ultra leaks have directed attention to the new camera island, but don’t overlook the missing camera lens left behind with the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Apparently, that camera is the Samsung Galaxy S27 Ultra’s 10MP 3x zoom.

We’ve seen a selection of leaks with details galore, including privacy displays, battery upgrades, and more. Any render that’s come out has shown off an entirely new camera island design, and it’s become the focus of the new phone. Love it or hate it, it’s there and almost square.

According to another leak via @UniverseIce on Twitter/X, the Galaxy S27 Ultra won’t have a 3x optical zoom lens with a 10MP sensor. Instead, the phone will have a wide 1x lens setup and a 5x optical zoom unit – 50MP, if left unchanged as suggested.

It is now confirmed that the Galaxy S27 Ultra will no longer have a 3× telephoto camera.

This means its rear camera system will jump directly from the 1× main camera to the 5× telephoto camera.

The main camera uses the ISOCELL HP6, essentially a Galaxy-customized version of the… https://t.co/qYGcdX93oy

— Ice Universe (@UniverseIce) September 29, 2026

The latest renders clearly show a missing lens if you compare the phone to last year’s model. The Galaxy S26 Ultra had a 3x and 5x optical zoom camera, totaling four sensors across the back of the phone. Now, sitting in a section of much larger real estate, the new camera array appears to have only three cameras.

	

A render posted by @OnLeaks labels portions of the new panel. Where previous renders showed another lens underneath the flash LED, this new render places the LED at the bottom, topped by additional sensors, a microphone, and what may now be the 5x zoom lens.

As is the case with nearly every Galaxy S series leak, these are to be taken with a grain of salt. Renders have come and gone, but we won’t know the final details until Samsung launches the device sometime in early 2027.

title: Google Antigravity Googlebook app hits the Play Store
snippet: Ahead of the Googlebook launch, Google Antigravity is now available in the Play Store. more…
fullText:
Ahead of the Googlebook launch, Google Antigravity is now available in the Play Store.

Antigravity is Google’s agent-first development platform, with version 2.0 released at I/O 2026 in May. It serves as a “dedicated mission control to work alongside, steer, and customize agents that operate autonomously in the background.”

After creating macOS, Windows, and Linux versions, Antigravity is now available on Android with a native interface. It interacts with the Linux environment available on the new laptops. You can “Create and deploy apps right on your Googlebook.”

The package name is com.google.android.apps.antigravity, and the app is currently on version 2026.09.23.988012583.

	

That said, it’s currently only available on Googlebook OS. The interface might work on tablets and foldables, but it’s unclear if Google designed it for smaller phone screens. 

The interface looks similar to the other desktop versions, but it remains to be seen whether it will retain feature parity given how quickly the other apps are updated with major features on a weekly basis.

Antigravity on Googlebooks is part of Google’s push to make the new platform suitable for developers. You can also just install the Linux version of Antigravity on Googlebooks, along with Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex. Additionally, Google advertised the ability to install the Antigravity CLI via the Googlebook terminal.

title: Apple among biggest corporate lobbyists in Brussels, per report
snippet: A new analysis by The Financial Times shows that Apple has met with EU policymakers 257 times since June 2024 and has spent between €8 million and €9 million per year on lobbying. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
A new analysis by The Financial Times shows that Apple has met with EU policymakers 257 times since June 2024 and has spent between €8 million and €9 million per year on lobbying. Here are the details.

Apple trails Google among major tech lobbyists in Brussels

In a report released today, The Financial Times (via MacMagazine) said that “Google, Apple and Amazon each have more meetings with officials at the European parliament and European Commission than any individual European company.”

According to the report, which is based on the bloc’s transparency register and meeting databases for the European Parliament and the European Commission, Apple spends €9 million a year on lobbying in the EU capital, more than what Total, Volkswagen, and Airbus spend combined. The FT notes that Meta’s yearly lobbying spending is even higher, at more than €10 million.

From the report:

American corporations have used their influence in Brussels to push back against the bloc’s digital rules, over which US President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened tariffs in response to Europe seeking “tech sovereignty” to reduce its reliance on US technology.

The FT gathered data from meetings held since June 2024, when the latest European Parliament elections took place, and found that Apple met with EU policymakers 257 times during that period. That put the company second only to Google among major tech companies, with 302 meetings.

Amazon also made the top 20, ranking 14th with 239 meetings, while WWF topped the overall list with 431, confirming The FT’s analysis that “green NGOs are the most active lobbyists.”

When asked about these efforts, Apple and Amazon reportedly told The FT that “they engage with policymakers on topics that are important to their customers and their businesses.”
